A study led by Iris Mauss, psychology professor at UC Berkeley, found that people who accept their sad or uncomfortable feelings experience fewer negative emotions overall.

Why does this happen? Researchers believe that when you allow emotions to exist, you give them less power. But when you judge your emotions harshly, the stress grows and stays longer.

What The Study Found

  • More than 1,300 adults were studied in California and Colorado.
  • People who avoided or judged their emotions felt more stress over time.
  • Those who allowed sadness, disappointment, or anger to run their course had fewer mood issues.
  • The benefits were visible even six months later.

According to lead author Brett Ford, accepting emotions helps people cope with stress better.

How They Tested It

  • Over 1,000 people answered questions about statements like “I shouldn’t feel this way.”
  • People who did not judge their emotions reported higher wellbeing.

Next, 150 people gave a stressful mock job speech. Those who normally suppress feelings felt more distress than people who accept their emotions.

Finally, 200 people journaled about stressful moments for two weeks. Six months later, those who avoided negative emotions showed more signs of mood problems.

What This Means For You

  • It’s okay to feel sad, angry, or disappointed.
  • Let emotions happen instead of fighting them.
  • Judging yourself for feeling bad makes things worse.

Researchers now want to explore how parenting, culture, and upbringing shape whether a person learns to accept emotions or suppress them.

Accepting your emotions doesn’t make you weak — it may make you mentally stronger.
author: Yasmin Anwar

title: Can reading improve your wellbeing?
header: Can a book do what social media can’t? Explore the hidden mental-health power of reading.
content:
Reading for Pleasure: Why It Matters

One in three adults in the UK rarely or never reads for pleasure. But reading for just 20 minutes a week can make you 20% more likely to feel satisfied with your life.

Many people can read but lose the habit due to major life changes, such as illness or having children. Two out of five people say they simply “don’t have time.”

Mood and Relaxation Benefits

  • Non-readers are 28% more likely to feel depressed.
  • 1 in 5 readers say reading helps them feel less lonely.
  • Reading has been shown to improve symptoms of depression.

Reading reconnects people with meaning, forgotten skills, and memories that build confidence and purpose.

Readers said reading relaxes them more than watching TV, scrolling social media, or reading magazines.

Reading helps the mind switch off gently by focusing attention and reducing everyday stress. 43% of readers say it helps them sleep better.

Stronger in Difficult Times

Reading helps people realise they are not alone. Many feel a sense of recognition — “this is me” — which builds resilience.

Regular readers say they cope better with setbacks and find it easier to make decisions and plan ahead.

Readers were also 18% more likely to report good self-esteem. Returning to reading often brings pride and a sense of achievement.

Better Connection With Others

  • Readers feel closer to friends and their communities.
  • Reading builds empathy and tolerance.
  • It gives richer topics to talk about and deeper conversations.

Readers understand more about social issues and cultural diversity. Their view of the world widens, and they feel more secure in it.

Reading for just 30 minutes a week makes you:

  • 52% more likely to feel socially included
  • 72% more likely to have community spirit
  • 37% more likely to enjoy social life more

Reading is not a luxury — it is support for life and well-being. Making time to read, even a little, truly matters.
author: Josie Billington

title: Listen To What You Are Saying
header: What if your inner voice is the only thing holding you back? Discover how to take the power back.
content:
The Power of Your Inner Voice

“If you hear a voice within you saying, ‘You are not a painter,’ then by all means paint, and that voice will be silenced.” – Vincent Van Gogh

We see ourselves through filters. Often these filters highlight negatives. As thoughts flow through these filters, they become words and inner conversations.

This inner voice affects your feelings, confidence, and actions. Only you can control it.

Your Inner Voice Shapes Your Actions

When you notice what you say to yourself, you understand why you react the way you do.

Example: Trying to help your child with maths but recalling past failures leads your inner voice to say “I am not good enough,” so you step back.

The problem is not maths — it is your self-concept.

Self-Concept Matters

Your self-concept is a mix of beliefs, memories, and opinions about yourself. It forms from both internal and external experiences.

You cannot change the past, but you can change how it influences your future.

Two Inner Dialogues After Failure

  • Positive version: “It hurts, but I worked hard. I will learn and find a better job.”
  • Negative version: “I failed because I am a loser. Nothing will work for me.”

Both situations are the same. But the conversation creates a different future.

First Step: Listen to Your Inner Voice

If your inner dialogue is full of doubt, it appears when you make important choices:

  • “You don’t deserve better.”
  • “Just accept what you get.”
  • “You are average.”

These messages slowly damage confidence — like termites.

Common Thinking Traps

Psychologist Harriet Braiker lists frequent inner-dialogue mistakes:

  • All-or-nothing: If it is not perfect, it is a failure.
  • Overgeneralizing: “Bad things always happen to me.”
  • Mental filter: Focus only on criticism.
  • Discounting positives: “Anyone could have done this.”
  • Jumping to conclusions: Assume failure without facts.
  • Magnification: Problems look bigger than they are.
  • Emotional reasoning: If I feel bad, I must be bad.
  • Labelling: “I am useless” instead of “I made a mistake.”
  • Personalization: Blame yourself for everything.

Build a Healthier Inner Voice

  • Notice your inner messages.
  • Challenge the negative ones.
  • Replace them with realistic, supportive thoughts.

When your inner dialogue supports you, it becomes a force for success, peace, and happiness.

title: Stress can age your brain. Here's why
header: Your brain may be older than your age… discover what’s speeding it up.
content:
How Stress Impacts Your Brain

Stress affects both physical and mental health. It increases risks of heart disease and depression.

Stressful Events Add Up

Researchers identified 27 life events that harm brain health. Examples include:

  • Being expelled from school
  • Losing a job

Each stressful event may age the brain by about 1.5 years.

Study Findings

Scientists asked 1,320 people to recall stressful experiences and take thinking tests.

Those with more stress scored lower, showing reduced memory and attention ability.

Why This Matters

The results may help identify people at risk for brain decline and guide early support.

How Stress Speeds Up Brain Ageing

Ageing naturally slows thinking, but stress can push this process faster.

Participants were only 58 years old on average, yet their stress levels already affected performance.

How Stress Harms the Brain

Long-term stress increases cortisol, which can:

  • Affect mood control
  • Increase blood pressure
  • Weaken immunity
  • Block learning and memory

The hippocampus, a memory area linked to Alzheimer’s, is especially affected.

Why Some People Are Hit Harder

Many factors shape stress effects, including:

  • Mental activity
  • Exercise habits
  • Nutrition

Healthy habits build “cognitive reserve,” helping protect the brain.

Stress and Inequality

Some groups face more stressful events. The study found African American participants experienced 60% more stress.

This led to stronger negative effects on memory and thinking.

Key Takeaway

Stress is common, but we can protect our brain with better habits and support systems.
author: Claire J. Hanley

title: Take A Break Before You Break Down
header: What happens to your mind when you never take time off? The truth hits hard.
content:
Why Taking Breaks Matters

Doing the same things every day can make anyone tired and unmotivated. When life feels repetitive, the mind becomes numb and creativity fades.

That is why breaks are important. Even a short pause helps your mind reset.

Why People Avoid Vacations

Many people hesitate to take longer breaks because they say:

  • No leave available
  • Too many deadlines
  • Limited money
  • Saving feels more important than travelling

But there will always be excuses. What matters is taking the break anyway so you return refreshed and productive.

Vacations do not need to be expensive. Even simple trips work if planned well.

Vacations Clear The Mind

Too much work—whether office tasks, studying, or parenting—creates mental clutter. Stepping away gives your brain time to breathe and return with clarity.

Holidays Boost Creativity

Many people get their best ideas while travelling. New places, cultures, and conversations inspire new thinking and fresh solutions.

Breaks Strengthen Relationships

Busy routines leave little time for family. Vacations give space to talk, bond, and understand each other better.

A strong home foundation supports a strong work life.

Final Thought

Plan a trip, even a simple one. Enjoy the break, recharge, and return ready for life again.

title: Values Parents Can Teach Children And Make Their Life Beautiful!
header: The parenting wisdom we all wish we learned earlier. Discover it now.
content:
Things Parents Can Teach Children for a Happy Life

Simple lessons can help children grow into kind, confident, and balanced human beings.

Become a Good Listener

“When you talk, you repeat what you know. When you listen, you learn.” – Dalai Lama

Listening builds patience and helps children solve problems calmly.

Happiness Over Marks

Inner peace helps children perform better. Guide them to seek wisdom, not just grades.

“Happiness is not a goal; it is a by-product.” – Eleanor Roosevelt

Do Not Be Judgmental

Teach children to understand others instead of judging them. Everyone has a different story.

“Never judge someone until you’ve walked a mile in their shoes.”

Sharing Is Caring

Giving makes people richer from within. Encourage children to share, even a little, every month.

“Happiness never decreases by being shared.” – Buddha

Personality Matters More Than Clothes

Guide children to value character over appearance or brand labels.

“I dress for comfort and style, not to impress.” – Lindsey Wixson

Turn Crisis Into Opportunity

Challenges often carry hidden opportunities. Teach children to stay calm and look for solutions.

“Failure is the chance to begin again, more intelligently.” – Henry Ford

Cultivate Positive Thoughts

Help children start their day with something uplifting. Positive minds create positive outcomes.

“Whoever is happy will make others happy too.” – Mark Twain

Forgive and Forget

Holding grudges drains energy. Teach children that forgiveness brings strength and peace.

“Forgiveness is the attribute of the strong.” – Mahatma Gandhi

Develop Trust and Bonding

Teach children to keep their good values even when others disappoint them.

“Better to trust the one who is often wrong than the one who is never in doubt.” – Eric Sevareid

Learn Money Management

Money buys comfort, not happiness. Teach children to spend wisely, save, and give to others.

“Every day is a bank account. Time is our currency.” – Christopher Rice

Final Message

If someone asks what you want your child to become, the answer is simple — a good human being.
author: Deepannita Das

title: How to turn your failures into success
header: Your biggest problems live in your head — and here’s how to stop them.
content:
Success After Failure

Everyone fails. The difference between success and struggle is how you respond to failure.

Obstacles can break you or become the story behind your success.

“There is no failure. Only feedback.” – Robert Allen

Failure Can Be a Teacher

With the right mindset, failure gives learning, direction, and new solutions.

What Research Shows

Psychologist Albert Bandura’s study revealed:

  • People who saw failure as proof of lack of ability gave up quickly.
  • People who saw failure as practice improved, grew confident, and performed better.

Your attitude decides whether failure stops you or strengthens you.

Lessons That Shape Success

The First Step Is the Hardest

Starting is scary, but action reduces fear. People who move first simply learned that doing beats waiting.

Good Things Take Time

Success demands effort and patience.

  • Henry Ford failed twice before launching Ford at 45.
  • Writer Harry Bernstein published a bestseller at 96.

Busy Is Not Productive

Success comes from focus, not running everywhere. You are measured by results, not effort.

You Control Less Than You Want

You cannot control everything, but you can control your reaction. This turns mistakes into lessons and success into humility.

You Are Who You Surround Yourself With

People who lift you help you grow. People who drain you hold you back. Let go of those who weaken your confidence.

Your Biggest Problems Are Mental

We get stuck in the past or fear the future. The only thing you can control is the present.

Self-Worth Must Come From Within

When your value depends on others, you lose control of your life. Appreciate yourself first; others’ opinions are secondary.

Not Everyone Will Support You

Many will doubt or criticize you. Don’t waste energy winning them over.

“Those who matter don’t mind, and those who mind don’t matter.” – Dr. Seuss

Perfection Doesn’t Exist

Seeking perfection leads to frustration. Focus on progress and what you learned.

Fear Creates the Deepest Regret

You will regret the chances you didn’t take more than your failures. Fear kills dreams before they begin.

Final Thought

Successful people keep learning—from mistakes and victories. Growth never stops, and every step improves you.
author: Travis Bradberry

title: Foolproof Ways To Lead An Unhappy Life
header: Are you accidentally destroying your own happiness? These hidden habits expose everything.
content:
Habits That Block Your Happiness

We all want to be happy, yet we often build habits that push us away from it. If you feel low or stuck, check whether any of these patterns are holding you back.

1. Amplifying Problems

Always complaining or feeling like a victim trains your mind to focus only on negatives. Change the story — act on the issue or adjust your attitude.

2. Hiding Your Problems

Ignoring problems does not solve them. Accepting an issue is the first step to healing it.

3. Making Unhealthy Comparisons

Wishing to be like someone else can slowly tell you “I am not good enough.”

  • List what you do have
  • Celebrate your wins — big and small
  • Love who you are

4. Expecting Too Much

When people do not meet your expectations, bitterness grows. Let happiness come from within — not from what others do for you.

5. Trying Too Hard to Please Everyone

You cannot make everyone happy. Changing yourself to win approval only harms your self-esteem.

  • Say no when needed
  • Stand by your opinions
  • Live for yourself

6. Holding On to Toxic Relationships

Some connections fade naturally. Others drain you or block your growth.

  • Accept when people change
  • Let go of bonds that bring more pain than joy
  • Create space for new, healthy relationships

Happiness grows when we drop habits that harm it — start small, stay aware, and choose yourself.

title: Why loneliness may be a greater public health hazard than obesity
header: Are we becoming the loneliest generation in history? The research says yes.
content:
The Rise of Loneliness

More people living alone, delaying marriage, and spending time on phones has led to a rise in loneliness in the United States.

Professor Julianne Holt-Lunstad of Brigham Young University shared research showing loneliness may be more dangerous than obesity and even similar to smoking risks.

What the Research Shows

  • 148 studies with over 300,000 people found that strong social connections reduce early death risk by 50%.
  • Another review of 3.4 million people found loneliness, living alone, and isolation increase death risk as much as or more than obesity.

Why Loneliness Hurts Health

Loneliness can lead to:

  • Poor sleep
  • High stress hormones
  • More inflammation
  • Weaker immunity

These factors increase chances of illness and serious health problems.

A Growing Issue

Over 42 million adults over age 45 in the U.S. suffer from chronic loneliness, and this is expected to grow as populations age.

How to Reduce Loneliness

  • Be proactive in meeting people.
  • Join clubs or community groups.
  • Plan time with family and neighbors.
  • Talk to doctors about loneliness risks.

Examples from Other Countries

England created a hotline called Silver Line where lonely seniors can call and talk about anything, anytime. The service receives about 10,000 calls weekly.

Loneliness may be rising, but small steps toward connection can protect our health and happiness.
author: Chris Weller

title: Living In The Present
header: Stuck between missing the past and fearing the future? Here’s what’s really going on.
content:
Living In The Present Moment

We often hear people say, “I wish I could go back to those days!” Childhood memories bring joy for many, and pain for some.

Looking at old photos reminds us of moments that shaped our lives — good or bad. Some wish to return to those worry-free days. Others would rather forget their early struggles.

Why We Miss The Past

As children, we wanted to grow up and gain freedom. Now that we are grown, we dream of going back to simple times.

The present often feels incomplete — we replay the past or chase the future, believing happiness lies anywhere but here.

The Important Truth

Right now is all we truly have.

  • We cannot change the past, but we can learn from it.
  • We cannot predict the future, but we can build toward it.

A Simple Example

I met a friend in college who was bullied as a child. Those past experiences made her believe she was unlovable, so she pushed people away — then wondered why she was alone.

Lessons To Remember

  • If your past was beautiful — cherish it.
  • If your past was painful — grow from it.
  • Do not let old wounds block trust, love, or opportunities.

It may be hard, but remember: sunshine follows rain, and strength is built from broken pieces.

Build From The Past, Live In The Now

The past is meant to teach us resilience so we can create a stronger future.

“If you’re depressed, you’re living in the past.
If you’re anxious, you’re living in the future.
If you’re at peace, you’re living in the present.” — Lao Tzu

title: Does Happiness Really Help You Live Longer?
header: A massive study says happiness won’t save your life — but here’s the twist you can’t ignore.
content:
Does Happiness Make Life Longer?

A new study suggests that happiness may not help you live longer. But when we look closer, the story is more complex.

For decades, research showed that happy people tend to live longer, healthier lives. But the UK Million Women Study reported something different. It studied nearly 720,000 women and found that people who said they felt happy “most of the time” did not live longer than those who said “rarely.”

Researchers concluded that poor health causes both unhappiness and early death — meaning health, not happiness, was the key factor.

But What Is Happiness?

Here’s the first issue — happiness means different things to different people. The study measured happiness by asking, “How often do you feel happy?”

That focuses only on short-term pleasure — joy, pride, excitement — which fades fast. This view treats happiness as something that simply happens to us.

Yet many philosophers, including Aristotle, say happiness is earned — built through meaning, purpose, and virtue.

A Deeper Kind of Happiness

Modern research agrees. Long-term happiness grows from:

  • Meaningful relationships
  • Kindness and generosity
  • Resilience
  • Awareness and purpose

These qualities can be developed over time — just like skills.

Different Emotions, Different Effects

Researchers also highlight that not all positive emotions are equal:

  • Short-lived pleasure feels good but fades quickly.
  • Pro-social emotions — gratitude, compassion, love — build stronger social bonds and may support long-term well-being.

This second type of happiness is linked to healthier bodies and minds.

Happiness Must Be Cultivated

Scientists now say lasting happiness grows from connection, belonging, and contribution.

  • Humans are wired to care, cooperate, and connect.
  • Positive social bonds help protect us from stress.
  • People report feeling happiest when spending time with others.
  • Generosity boosts happiness across cultures.
  • Loneliness harms immunity, heart health, and mood.

This suggests that poor social well-being can reduce happiness and also damage health.

A Flaw in the Study

The Million Women Study did ask about social life — like living with a partner or joining group activities — but then removed these factors from their analysis.

So, the only happiness measured was how often people felt momentary pleasure — not deeper life satisfaction.

So Does Happiness Matter?

Yes — but not just fleeting good feelings.

The kind of happiness that comes from meaning, relationships, and kindness is the one linked to health and longevity.

That is the happiness worth building.
author: EMILIANA R. SIMON-THOMAS

title: Do you need to rethink your definition of success?
header: You’re not failing — you’re using the wrong definition of success. Here’s the truth.
content:
Rethinking What Success Really Means

Today, many people believe success means fame, wealth, big jobs, or a top university degree. But this belief is misleading and damaging.

Many people tie their worth to achievements. When they win, they feel valuable. When they fail, they feel empty and broken.

A better view of success is becoming a wise, kind, and helpful human being. This kind of success brings meaning, resilience, and peace.

The Meaning of Success

Psychologist Erik Erikson said each stage of life teaches us something:

  • Teen years: build identity
  • Young adulthood: build close relationships
  • Adulthood: help and support others

The last stage is called generativity — contributing to others, guiding younger people, and making something useful for the world.

A story Erikson shared explains this. A dying man, surrounded by family, suddenly asked, “Who is minding the store?” Adult life, he implied, is about helping the world keep running for future generations.

Real success is not about winning. It is about serving.

A Modern Example

Anthony Tjan once believed success meant fame and money. After his company lost its chance to go public, he felt crushed.

With time, he realized he was chasing the wrong goal. He now defines success as using your strengths to serve a higher purpose.

Today, he invests in businesses that improve people’s lives, including one that gives fair pay and benefits to salon workers.

He says, “I want my children to pursue wholeness, not winning.”

Why Being Useful Matters

Feeling useless damages happiness. Feeling needed and helpful builds purpose.

In a long study of adult development:

  • A writer who was invited to teach said it confirmed his usefulness.
  • A man who was unemployed felt worthless and ashamed.

Being able to contribute is not just economic — it is emotional and deeply human.

Work Is Not the Only Way

Another man in the study had awards, high positions, and recognition. But inside, he felt empty.

He realized his success never helped others, and what he really wanted was meaning — not applause.

Later, he shifted his focus to:

  • Being a better father
  • Mentoring younger people
  • Supporting his community

His success became the ways he contributed, not the praise he received.

What This Teaches Us

Many of us will not achieve every dream. The real question is: how do we respond?

We can call ourselves failures, or we can redefine success.

True success is being useful — helping others, nurturing relationships, and improving the world around us.

This kind of success brings meaning and lasts long after our achievements are forgotten.
author: Emily Esfahani Smith

title: Ways To Bounce Back In Life When Failure Knocks You Down
header: This simple mindset hack can turn your worst defeat into your greatest momentum.
content:
How to Bounce Back After Failure

You tried something important – a test, a job, a relationship – and it didn’t work out. Now you have two choices:

  • Sit, complain, and change nothing.
  • Stand up, learn, and bounce back.

If you are reading this, you’ve already chosen to bounce back. Here are 10 simple, beginner-friendly steps to help you start again with confidence.

1. Tell Yourself: I CAN and I WILL

Every morning, remind yourself:

“Today is a new day. I cannot change my past, but I can act today and shape my future.”

Say it often. Write it down. Your words train your mind.

2. Make a Clear Plan

Whatever your goal is – passing an exam, getting a job, losing weight, learning a skill – you need a plan, not just hope.

  • Talk to people who have done it before.
  • Watch videos, read simple guides or books.
  • Write a basic step-by-step plan that fits your time, resources, and strengths.

3. Break Your Goal into Small Parts

Big goals can feel scary. Break them into small daily or weekly steps.

Example: You want to run a 5K race in 4 weeks.

  • Week 1: Walk or jog 3 times a week.
  • Week 2: Jog every day with short water breaks.
  • Week 3: Focus on breathing and running a bit longer.
  • Week 4: Practice and repeat – build confidence.
  • Race day: Enjoy what you trained for.

4. Stop Waiting for “Tomorrow”

The biggest mistake is thinking, “I still have time.” Time goes fast. If you delay today, it becomes easier to delay again tomorrow.

  • Set a small target for each day.
  • Finish that target before you sleep.
  • Don’t aim for perfect – aim for done.

Each day you keep your promise to yourself, your confidence grows.

5. Celebrate Small Wins

Don’t wait for the final big success to feel proud. Every small step matters.

  • Completed your task for the day? Smile. Mark it as done.
  • Stuck to your plan for a week? Treat yourself to something simple.

These small celebrations tell your mind: “I am making progress. I can do this.”

6. Be the “Deaf Frog”

There is a story of a frog that climbed a tall tree while other frogs shouted, “You can’t do it!” It reached the top because it was deaf and couldn’t hear them.

Learn from this:

  • Ignore unnecessary negative comments.
  • Don’t seek approval from everyone.
  • Spend more time with people who motivate you, not those who pull you down.

7. Cut Distractions, Focus on Your Goal

Today we are flooded with information – social media, chats, videos, notifications. Most of it is not useful for your goal.

  • Limit time on social media and messaging apps.
  • Use your free time to walk, play, talk to real friends, or read.
  • Ask yourself: “Is this helping my goal or just wasting my time?”

Important news will reach you eventually. Your focus is more valuable.

8. Don’t Compare Yourself to Others

Your life is unique. You can never be someone else, and they can never be you.

  • Everyone has different starting points and backgrounds.
  • The best results don’t always come from the best resources.
  • They come from the best attitude and steady effort.

Focus on becoming a better you, not a copy of someone else.

9. Face Your Weaknesses

Everyone has strengths and weaknesses. It’s normal.

  • List what you are good at – use these strengths.
  • List what you struggle with – work on them slowly.
  • Don’t run away from your weak areas; they grow bigger when you avoid them.

When you face a weak spot and improve even a little, your confidence jumps.

10. Look Back and See How Far You’ve Come

From time to time, pause and ask:

  • Where did I start?
  • What problems have I already overcome?
  • What small wins have I collected?

You’ll see that your progress is not an accident. You came this far because of your effort and courage.

There is no better day than today to start again.
Stay patient, stay positive, and keep moving. Your “bounce back” story is already in progress.
author: Ananya

title: Four Awe-Inspiring Activities
header: A single awe-filled moment can lower inflammation. Here’s how to create one today.
content:
How to Feel More Awe in Everyday Life

When was the last time you felt truly amazed by something? Children feel awe often, but adults are usually busy with daily tasks and worries. Still, awe is very important for adults too.

What Is Awe?

Awe is the feeling you get when you face something bigger than yourself that changes how you see the world.

  • A beautiful view, like mountains or the ocean
  • A great work of art or music
  • A moving speech
  • A special moment, like a baby’s first steps

Awe often makes you feel small, but not in a bad way. It helps you feel connected to other people and to something bigger than your daily life. When you feel awe, your problems can seem smaller and easier to handle.

Why Awe Is Good for You

Research shows that awe has many benefits:

  • More life satisfaction
  • A feeling that time is slower and more open
  • More kindness and desire to help others
  • Less stress and more curiosity
  • Possible health benefits, like lower inflammation in the body

You do not need to feel awe all the time. But adding a bit more awe to your life can make you happier and more calm.

Simple Awe Practices

Here are four easy ways to bring more awe into your daily life.

1. Write About a Personal Awe Moment

Think about a time in your life when you felt deep wonder, such as:

  • A walk through a huge canyon or forest
  • Seeing a famous place, like the pyramids of Egypt
  • Watching your child take their first steps

Then try this simple writing exercise:

  • Close your eyes and remember the moment in detail.
  • Write about what you saw, heard, and felt.
  • Describe the place, the people, and your emotions.

Studies show that writing about awe can:

  • Increase feelings of awe
  • Reduce the sense of time pressure
  • Make you more willing to help others

This is a good practice when daily life feels heavy or boring. Remembering a powerful moment can remind you that the world can be magical.

2. Take an “Awe Walk”

You do not have to travel far to feel awe. You can find it close to home with an Awe Walk.

Choose a place that might inspire you, such as:

  • A park, forest, or tree-lined path
  • A high place with a wide view, like a hill or tall building
  • A museum or beautiful building

During your Awe Walk, try to:

  • Look at your surroundings as if it’s your first time there.
  • Notice small details, like the color of the sky or a bird’s song.
  • Leave your phone and other distractions at home if possible.
  • Try new routes so you see fresh sights and sounds.

Even a familiar walk can feel different if you pay attention in a new way. Research shows that people who look at tall trees and nature, even for a short time, feel more awe, more humble, and are more likely to help others.

3. Watch an Awe-Inspiring Video

You can also find awe on your screen. The internet is full of powerful images and videos.

Some ideas:

  • Nature videos with mountains, oceans, or space
  • Documentaries from places like National Geographic
  • Inspiring speeches or performances on video platforms
  • Your own photos or videos from past trips

To use videos for awe:

  • Pick a short video that feels big, beautiful, or mind-opening.
  • Watch it with full attention (no multitasking).
  • Notice how your body and emotions feel while watching.

Studies show that people who watch awe videos feel more awe, feel like they have more time, and sometimes become more generous.

4. Read an Awe-Inspiring Story

Words can also create awe in your mind. One simple practice is to read a story that puts you in a powerful scene, like standing on top of the Eiffel Tower and looking at the whole city below.

You can find awe in:

  • Stories that describe amazing views or experiences
  • Science books, like A Brief History of Time by Stephen Hawking
  • Your own writing about past awe moments

To use stories for awe:

  • Choose a story that feels big, beautiful, or mind-opening.
  • Read slowly and imagine that you are inside the story.
  • Notice how it changes your mood and sense of time.

Research shows that reading awe stories can increase life satisfaction, make people value experiences more than things, and give a feeling of having more time.

Making Life More “Awesome”

Some days, life feels dull and tiring. On those days, a small moment of awe can lift your mood and remind you of your purpose.

  • Awe can feel strange or even a little scary sometimes.
  • But it can also break routine and help you see life in a new way.
  • You can find awe in nature, art, memories, videos, stories, and more.

Try one small awe practice this week—write about a special moment, take an Awe Walk, watch a powerful video, or read an inspiring story. Tiny moments of awe can slowly make your life more “awesome.”

title: Ways to Start your Sustainable Lifestyle Journey
header: Want a healthier planet and a happier life? These habits make it surprisingly simple
content:
Simple Guide to Sustainable Living

Many of us hear about “sustainability,” but it can be hard to understand what it really means. In simple terms, sustainability is the ability to live well today without harming the future. It means saving resources so future generations can enjoy them too.

Environmental sustainability is a key part of this idea. It means using natural resources in a way that does not damage the planet. You don’t need to give up comfort—just be more mindful of how you use things.

Easy Tips to Live More Sustainably

1. The Power to Power Off

Small actions can save energy:

  • Turn off lights and appliances when not in use
  • Use energy-saving bulbs like LEDs
  • Try solar chargers when possible

2. Step Up Your Transportation

Ask yourself if you really need a car for every trip:

  • Use public transport when possible
  • Try walking or cycling—they are healthy too!

3. Eat Consciously

Your food choices matter:

  • Try eating more plant-based meals
  • Use reusable or biodegradable containers
  • Carry your own bottle or food box

4. Wear Green on Wednesdays

The fashion industry creates lots of pollution. You can help by:

  • Shopping less and choosing quality over quantity
  • Recycling or donating clothes
  • Supporting eco-friendly and cruelty-free brands

5. Say No to Plastic

Living plastic-free is hard, but you can start small:

  • Refuse plastic bags and bottles
  • Switch to reusable bags and containers
  • Try making your own simple products over time

Sustainable living does not happen overnight. Small steps add up and make a big difference. Start today, and over time you will see how rewarding it can be—for you and for the planet.

title: Meditation could make your brain much younger, according to this research
header: Your brain can literally grow younger — explore the simple habit behind it.
content:
How Meditation Changes Your Brain

Neuroscientist Sara Lazar from Mass General and Harvard Medical School discovered meditation by accident. She began yoga only to help her running injuries. But something surprising happened — she started feeling calmer, kinder, and more open-minded.

Curious, she looked into research and found strong evidence: meditation reduces stress, anxiety, depression, pain, and insomnia, while increasing overall quality of life.

What the Research Shows

Lazar began studying the brain changes caused by meditation.

Study 1: Long-Term Meditators

She compared people who had meditated for 7–9 years with non-meditators.

  • They had more gray matter in areas tied to hearing, sensing, and awareness.
  • They also had more gray matter in the frontal cortex — linked to decision-making and memory.
  • Most people lose gray matter with age, but 50-year-old meditators had the same amount as 25-year-olds.

This suggests meditation may help protect the brain as we age.

Study 2: Beginners After 8 Weeks

To check if people were “born” this way, she ran another test with beginners.

After just 8 weeks of meditation, brain changes appeared:

  • Growth in the hippocampus (learning, memory, emotional balance)
  • Growth in the TPJ (empathy, perspective-taking)
  • Growth in the brainstem pons (regulates neurotransmitters)
  • Shrinkage in the amygdala (fear, stress, and anxiety center)

The smaller amygdala matched lower stress levels — meaning people actually felt calmer.

How Long Do You Need to Meditate?

In the study, people were told to meditate for 40 minutes daily.

  • The average ended up being 27 minutes a day
  • Other studies suggest 15–20 minutes daily can bring benefits

Lazar herself says her practice varies: sometimes 40 minutes, sometimes 5 minutes, sometimes not at all — like exercise, doing “a little every day” still helps.

The Takeaway

  • Meditation can slow aging in your brain
  • Even beginners see results in weeks
  • Small, consistent practice matters more than perfection

Meditation may not give you the body of a 25-year-old — but it might give your brain the power of one!
author: Melanie Curtin

title: Better Way to Pursue Happiness
header: Happiness isn’t about constant joy. Discover the method that really boosts well-being.
content:
How to Pursue Happiness the Right Way

Everyone wants to be happy. Research shows happiness boosts health and can even improve earnings. But chasing happiness the wrong way may actually make us feel worse.

Studies show that trying too hard to “feel happy” in every moment can backfire. Instead, the key may be how we pursue happiness — not how much we want it.

The Trap of Forcing Happiness

People who try to feel happy all the time often end up disappointed. Constantly checking how happy you are can actually push happiness away.

Writer Ruth Whippman even described happiness chasing as a “recipe for stress.” But research suggests there is a healthier way to pursue happiness.

Prioritizing Positivity

A more effective strategy is called “prioritizing positivity.” This means planning your life so you regularly do things that naturally make you feel good.

  • Make time for hobbies you enjoy
  • Spend time with people who uplift you
  • Choose jobs or activities that create positive emotions

Instead of forcing yourself to “feel happy,” you put yourself in situations where happiness arises naturally.

What the Research Found

Researchers developed a quiz to measure how much people prioritize positive experiences.

People who scored high on prioritizing positivity:

  • Experienced more positive emotions
  • Had fewer negative emotions
  • Reported more life satisfaction
  • Showed fewer depression symptoms

On the other hand, people who obsessively valued happiness:

  • Felt fewer positive emotions
  • Had more negative emotions
  • Reported lower life satisfaction
  • Had more depression symptoms

Both groups cared about happiness — but only one approach worked well.

How to Pursue Happiness More Effectively

1. Let Go of Unrealistic Expectations

  • You do not need to feel happy all the time.
  • Negative emotions help us learn and grow.
  • Life will always include stress — and that’s okay.

Trying to monitor your happiness every moment actually blocks joy and prevents “flow” — the deep focus that brings real happiness.

2. Identify What Brings You Joy

Think about activities that make you feel peaceful or fulfilled:

  • Cooking or gardening
  • Sports, reading, or arts
  • Connecting with family or friends

Research shows two activities boost happiness for most people:

  • Spending time with loved ones
  • Doing something physically active

3. Schedule Happiness Into Your Week

  • Plan your joyful activities — don’t wait for spare time.
  • Turn them into commitments — for example, walking with a friend.
  • Small routines, even 15–20 minutes a day, can lift your mood.

The Takeaway

Happiness is not about forcing good feelings or chasing constant joy. Instead, create a life filled with small moments that bring positive emotions.

Adjust your routine, add activities you enjoy, and let happiness unfold naturally. Pursuing happiness may be delicate — but it is still worth it.
author: LAHNNA CATALINO

title: Things You Are Scared Of But You Should Do It Anyway
header: Afraid of losing people? Why courage is the only way to keep what matters.
content:
It’s Okay to Be Scared — Do It Anyway

They say, “Don’t let fear of what could happen make nothing happen.” Fear is real, and you can’t always ignore it. So face it, challenge it, and grow beyond it.

Movies often inspire us. One powerful example is Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara. The moment Hrithik’s character dives underwater — terrified but transformed — reminds us that overcoming fear brings peace and growth.

Many of us are scared — of change, of challenges, of stepping outside comfort. And that’s okay.

1. Your Comfort Zone

Life inside comfort feels safe. Stepping out can be scary — the world can be unpredictable.

  • It’s okay to fear leaving what you know.
  • The world outside also has beauty and opportunity.
  • If something helps you grow, take the leap anyway.

You may surprise yourself and feel like a hero in your own eyes.

2. Fear of Losing People

Friends matter. Sometimes you need difficult conversations — even when you fear losing someone.

  • Speak your truth.
  • Be vulnerable.
  • Your relationships deepen when you face fears instead of hiding.

3. Fear of Failure and Limits

Everyone has limits, but letting fear control you is the real failure.

  • Push beyond what feels safe.
  • You will fall — and learn.
  • What you become through struggle will lift you up.

4. Fear of the Past

The past can leave deep marks. But it does not have to define you.

  • Face painful memories instead of running.
  • Forgive yourself and move forward.
  • Create new stories — with new courage.

5. Fear of Dreaming

Dream boldly — with your eyes open.

  • Dreams will challenge your skills — that’s the point.
  • Ask for help, fail, get up, and keep going.
  • Move toward your dream step by step.

The Final Thought

Fear will always be there. Feel it — but don’t let it stop you. It’s okay to be scared. Do it anyway.
author: Gargee Dutta

title: Lifestyle changes that could boost your mood and mental health
header: Feeling low? Science says these simple habits can change your mood fast.
content:
Simple Lifestyle Changes for Better Mental Health

When someone is diagnosed with anxiety or depression, treatment often includes therapy and medication. But everyday habits also play a big role in how we feel mentally — even for people without a mental health condition.

Small, meaningful changes can improve mood, reduce stress, and support overall well-being. Here are five simple lifestyle steps to get started:

1. Improve Your Diet and Get Moving

Food fuels your brain. Try adding more:

  • Leafy greens, whole grains, legumes
  • Lean meats, fish, and seafood
  • Berries, tea, dark chocolate, and herbs

Exercise is also powerful — swimming, jogging, weights, team sports, or even brisk walking can boost mood. Activities done outdoors or with others offer extra benefits.

  • Aim for about 30 minutes most days (150 minutes weekly).
  • Even short bursts of movement can lift your mood immediately.

2. Reduce Unhealthy Habits

Alcohol and drug misuse can worsen mental health. While some studies hint at small benefits from light drinking, newer findings suggest no real brain benefit.

  • Consider cutting back on alcohol if it affects your mood.
  • Quitting smoking improves mood and reduces anxiety over time.

Your brain adjusts — even if withdrawal feels tough at first.

3. Prioritize Rest and Sleep

Good sleep supports emotional balance. Try these habits:

  • Limit caffeine later in the day
  • Keep a regular sleep schedule
  • Get up at the same time each morning
  • Avoid forcing sleep — get up briefly if you can’t fall asleep
  • Reduce screen time and blue light before bed

Relaxation, hobbies, and downtime are just as important for managing stress.

4. Get Some Nature Time

Sunshine boosts serotonin and vitamin D — both linked to mood and sleep.

  • Spend time outdoors when you can.
  • Balance sun exposure with skin safety.
  • Limit toxins, noise, and excess screen time.

Time in nature — even short visits — can improve mood and self-esteem. Pets and animal-assisted activities also offer emotional benefits.

5. Reach Out When You Need Help

Lifestyle changes support mental health, but they don’t replace therapy or medication.

  • Some changes are hard — especially if habits act as emotional crutches.
  • Seek support if quitting or changing behaviour feels overwhelming.
  • Avoid strict or guilt-driven rules — go gently with yourself.

Notice how you feel after a good meal, quality sleep, or a walk in nature with someone you care about. Small choices can add up to big improvements.
author: Jerome Sarris

title: Why Laughter is Contagious
header: Your laughter is more powerful than you think — even chimps use it to build trust.
content:
Why Contagious Laughter Matters — Even for Chimps

We all know laughter is contagious — it spreads through movie theaters, classrooms, and even business meetings. But new research shows this contagious laughter may have deep evolutionary roots.

Chimps Laugh Just Like Us

A recent study published in the journal Emotion found that chimpanzees — our close animal relatives — imitate each other’s laughter, just like humans do.

This type of “polite” or responsive laughter happens even when the second chimp isn’t feeling exactly the same emotion. Similar patterns are seen in people — when someone laughs, we often laugh back.

The Study

Researchers observed 59 chimpanzees living in a sanctuary in Zambia.

  • Two groups were new communities (together for only five years)
  • Two were long-term colonies (living together for over 14 years)

When chimps played together, one chimp’s laugh often triggered a shorter, differently toned laugh from the partner. This responsive laugh strengthened play and bonding — the pairs played longer when laughter was shared.

Why It Matters

  • The study shows chimps use laughter to build social connection.
  • This mirrors human conversational laughter.
  • Newer social groups imitated laughter more, possibly to build trust.

Researchers believe this contagious laughter offered major advantages to our ancestors — helping groups cooperate, communicate, and bond.

The Bigger Picture

According to lead researcher Davila-Ross, laughter may have first evolved as a way for apes to communicate positively and build relationships. Over time, humans expanded its use — for joy, connection, and even teasing or mocking.

So the next time laughter spreads across a room — even in a business meeting — remember: it isn’t just fun. It’s a deeply wired social tool that humans share with chimps, designed to help us connect.

title: Happy People Don’t Need to Feel Superior
header: Science says happy people don’t fear comparison — here’s the habit that protects them.
content:
Why Happy People Choose Good Company

A new study suggests happy people avoid getting stuck in social comparison. Like good leaders, they don’t fear being around people who might outperform them — they actually seek it out and benefit from it.

What the Study Found

Researchers asked students in Korea to imagine scoring poorly on a test and receiving a message from a friend who either:

  • Did better on the test and was happy, or
  • Did worse and was generally unhappy

Happy students were more eager to spend time with the happy, higher-scoring friend and believed they would feel better afterward. Unhappy students didn’t show a preference.

Is Self-Esteem the Real Reason?

Researchers wondered if confident people — who often feel happier — simply don’t get intimidated. But even after controlling for self-esteem, happy people still preferred spending time with happy-but-superior friends.

This result also appeared in a U.S. sample, showing the pattern exists across cultures.

Does Misery Love Company?

The researchers tested one more theory: that unhappy people may prefer other unhappy people because it comforts them.

Students were asked to choose between:

  • A happy but poor-performing friend, or
  • An unhappy but successful friend

Both happy and unhappy students preferred the happy friend — regardless of performance. Misery, it turns out, did not love company.

Why Happy People Make Good Friends

Research shows that happy people are:

  • More helpful and generous
  • More cooperative and sociable
  • Friendlier and more attentive
  • More likely to view others positively

Their upbeat mood can rub off on us, improving our own emotional state.

How Happy People Stay Happy

Happy people seem to choose emotionally resourceful companions — people who uplift them and perform well. This choice may help them maintain their own well-being and success.

But there is another takeaway: noticing our natural bias for positive people can help us make intentional choices. Spending time with unhappy friends may benefit them — as long as we also balance our own emotional needs.

As the researchers put it, happy people are wise about whom they spend time with. They simply choose well — and that keeps them happy.
author: KIRA M. NEWMAN

title: Secrets to happiness, according to Roman Stoics
header: Feeling overwhelmed? Discover the ancient mindset that instantly changes everything.
content:
What the Roman Stoics Can Teach Us Today

We may thank the Romans for their roads — but they also left lessons for life in the 21st century. Three major Stoic thinkers — Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius — offer guidance that still speaks today.

Modern books such as The Daily Stoic and Stoicism and the Art of Happiness show how their teachings help people live happier and calmer lives. There is even an annual week dedicated to Stoicism.

What Is Stoicism?

Stoicism teaches that a good life comes from having a strong, rational mind. Happiness comes from living in harmony with nature and staying calm about things outside our control.

The early Stoics lived in Greece, but it was the Roman philosophers who left writings that shaped the modern world.

1. Control How You Think

Epictetus taught two key ideas. First, some things are in our control — and most things are not.

  • We cannot control events around us.
  • We cannot control other people.
  • We cannot even fully control our bodies.

The only thing we fully control is how we think — the judgments we make about situations.

His second principle: our emotions come not from events but from our judgments about them.

  • If we judge something as terrible, we feel upset.
  • If we expect something bad, we feel fear.
  • What scares one person may not bother another.

The good news? Judgments are fully within our control — meaning our happiness can be too.

2. Train Your Mind

Stoics understood that life is difficult. Seneca himself suffered exile, loss, and was ordered to die by Nero.

They knew it is hard to stay calm — so they created exercises to help:

  • Seneca suggested reviewing your day and noticing where emotions tripped you.
  • Marcus Aurelius prepared himself each morning by expecting difficult people.

By practicing awareness, Stoics aimed to respond wisely rather than react emotionally.

3. Accept What Happens

Stoics also remind us that we are small in a vast universe. Marcus Aurelius reflected on the endless stretch of time to keep his worries in perspective.

From this view, expecting life to go exactly how we want seems unreasonable.

  • If we demand the universe to meet our wishes, we suffer.
  • If we accept what life brings, we find peace.

Many people today are practicing this mindset — working to accept rather than resist life’s challenges.

The Takeaway

Stoicism teaches that while we control very little, we can fully control how we think — and that may be the secret to lasting happiness.
author: John Sellars

title: This is how important sleep is for your mental health
header: Why messing with your sleep-wake cycle may be hurting your mind more than you think.
content:
How Your Body Clock Affects Mental Health

If you’ve ever taken a long flight or worked a night shift, you may have felt moody, tired, or unfocused. These changes come from disruptions in your body’s sleep-wake cycle — your circadian rhythm. New research shows that disturbing this rhythm may increase the risk of depression and bipolar disorder.

What Are Circadian Rhythms?

Circadian rhythms are 24-hour patterns in your body — affecting temperature, hormones, sleep, and activity. They play a key role in both physical and mental health.

What the Study Found

Many earlier studies relied on self-reported sleep data and small samples. But a new study in The Lancet Psychiatry used:

  • Over 91,000 UK participants
  • Objective tracking using wrist-worn monitors
  • Controls for other influences like age, lifestyle, smoking, trauma, and BMI

The results were clear:

  • People with disrupted rhythms — active at night or inactive during the day — had higher risk of mood disorders.
  • They reported lower well-being and slower thinking or reaction speed.

These effects were not explained by lifestyle or background factors.

Why This Matters

The findings support the idea that disturbed circadian rhythms are linked to poor mental health. They also show that simple activity tracking could help identify people at risk of depression or bipolar disorder.

A Global Challenge

Modern life makes this problem worse:

  • Artificial light — especially at night — disrupts natural rhythms.
  • Urban living exposes millions to constant light and noise.

By 2030, two-thirds of the world will live in cities — meaning more people may face disrupted rhythms and higher risk of mental health challenges.

What We Still Don’t Know

The study can’t tell us whether:

  • Disrupted rhythms cause mental illness, or
  • Mood disorders disrupt rhythms, or
  • Both are influenced by genes or shared environments.

Long-term studies tracking the same people will help answer these questions. Researchers also want to test whether stabilising sleep patterns can improve symptoms.

The Big Takeaway

We’ve long known sleep affects physical health — now science shows it’s deeply tied to mental health too.

Understanding and protecting our circadian rhythm may become a key part of treating depression, bipolar disorder, and improving overall well-being.
author: Daniel Smith, Laura Lyall

title: Why Self-Compassion Trumps Self-Esteem
header: Stop judging yourself: this research-backed habit brings more calm than success ever could.
content:
Why Being Kind to Yourself Matters

Researcher Kristin Neff shows that treating yourself with compassion leads to less anxiety, less conflict, and more peace of mind.

The Problem With Constant Self-Judgment

In a competitive world, many people struggle to feel good about themselves. We compare, criticize, and try to stand out — but this usually backfires.

  • We inflate our egos to feel worthier than others.
  • We avoid admitting flaws because truth feels painful.
  • The result is insecurity, stress, and emotional exhaustion.

When self-evaluation collapses, many people fall into despair: “I’m not good enough” or “I’m worthless.”

There Is Another Way

Instead of judging ourselves, Neff suggests we stop labeling ourselves as good or bad — and treat ourselves with the same warmth we would offer a friend.

This idea — self-compassion — changed Neff’s life while she was struggling with divorce and shame. She learned we are allowed to show kindness to ourselves when we fail or suffer.

At first she feared compassion would make her lazy or selfish. But she realized self-criticism only fueled insecurity, poor relationships, and fear of telling the truth.

Self-Compassion vs. Self-Esteem

After studying self-esteem, Neff concluded:

  • Self-esteem protects us only when we feel successful.
  • It can lead to arrogance, anger, or prejudice.
  • Self-compassion gives the same emotional protection — without ego traps.

Self-compassion lets us feel worthy even when we fall short.

The Three Parts of Self-Compassion

  • Self-kindness: Be gentle, not harsh, with yourself.
  • Common humanity: Remember everyone struggles — you are not alone.
  • Mindfulness: Notice your pain without exaggerating or ignoring it.

Unlike self-esteem, compassion does not depend on being special or perfect.

What the Research Shows

Studies reveal clear benefits:

  • Less anxiety, depression, and negativity
  • More happiness, optimism, and resilience
  • Healthier responses to failure or criticism

In one study, self-compassionate students felt less anxious during mock job interviews — because they were not afraid to admit weaknesses.

Other studies show self-compassion:

  • Reduces embarrassment and self-blame
  • Helps people take mistakes in stride
  • Makes feelings of self-worth more stable over time
  • Decreases social comparison and defensiveness
  • Is not linked to narcissism (unlike self-esteem)

An Island of Calm

Self-compassion creates emotional safety — a place where you no longer obsess over whether you are “good enough.”

By accepting imperfections and treating yourself with kindness, you can feel more secure, connected, and alive.

It takes practice to quiet a lifetime of self-criticism, but the invitation is simple: relax, allow life to be imperfect, and open your heart to yourself.

It may be easier — and more life-changing — than you think.
author: KRISTIN NEFF

title: Boost Your Habits of Helping
header: How focusing on giving—not getting—quietly upgrades your entire emotional life.
content:
Simple Ways to Notice and Grow Your Habit of Helping

Here are easy practices to recognize how you already support others — and to expand your kindness even more.

1. Keep a Giving Journal

Once a week, write down the big and small ways you helped others.

  • A smile
  • A kind question
  • Picking up groceries
  • Offering support or listening

If you can’t think of examples, ask someone close — you may be surprised at how much you already do.

2. Help One Person Every Day

Make kindness a daily habit. Try small acts like:

  • Holding the elevator
  • Helping with a chore
  • Giving food or support to someone in need

Research shows regular acts of kindness boost happiness over time. Try different levels and find what works for you.

3. Visualize Helping

Each morning, close your eyes and imagine yourself helping people you will meet that day.

This mental “priming” increases the odds you’ll act kindly when the moment arrives.

4. Use Your Natural Talents

You help best when you draw on your strengths.

  • Are you good at listening?
  • Do you enjoy problem-solving?
  • Do you love cooking, teaching, organizing, or fixing things?

Helping through your passions keeps you motivated and consistent.

5. Reflect on What Others Have Given You

Think about people who have supported or uplifted you.

  • Offer thanks — even a simple message matters.
  • Consider writing a gratitude letter and delivering it in person.

Research shows this can increase happiness for weeks.

6. Try Concentric Visualizations

Close your eyes and imagine smiling warmly at:

  • Someone you love
  • A casual acquaintance
  • Someone you believe truly needs help

Picture them smiling back — then think of one real way you could help that last person today.

With practice, these small steps can grow your kindness, deepen relationships, and brighten your days.

title: Things everyone needs to know about happiness
header: Happiness isn’t luck—discover the choices happy people make every day.
content:
Share Happiness: What Truly Makes Us Happier

The International Day of Happiness reminds us to focus on relationships, kindness, and helping one another. Life includes grief and struggle, but we can always learn, grow, and move forward.

Here are five ideas that help explain what increases happiness:

1. Believe in Free Will

People who believe they can make their own choices tend to feel happier. Even if the past influences us, believing we have control gives us more confidence and a positive outlook.

2. It’s Not All About Money

Money improves life comfort — food, leisure, and stability matter. But research shows a “satiation point,” where more money no longer increases happiness. In some cases, life satisfaction drops due to pressure and stress.

3. Serve Others

Buddhist monk Matthieu Ricard — sometimes called “the happiest man alive” — teaches that happiness comes from personal growth and helping others. When we contribute to others’ well-being, we transform ourselves.

4. Measure GNH, Not GDP

Bhutan measures Gross National Happiness instead of just economic output. Government policies must pass a happiness test — if they won’t improve well-being, they are changed. This shifts national priorities toward balance and fulfillment.

5. Copy the Nordics

Finland ranks first in the World Happiness Report, with other Nordic nations close behind.

  • Safe, stable society
  • Work-life balance
  • Strong education and childcare
  • Trusted governments and low corruption

They value freedom, fairness, and quality of life. Even if moving there isn’t possible, we can learn from their practices.

Happiness grows when we support others, value balance, and build communities where people can live well — together.
author: Briony Harris

title: Here's how you can keep yourself staying positive
header: Science explains why your mind spirals—and how to stop it before it starts.
content:
How to Stay Positive When Your Mind Wants to Worry

We often hear “stay positive,” but when life is stressful, positivity can feel unrealistic. Our brains naturally scan for danger — this helped our ancestors survive, but today it often creates unnecessary fear and negativity.

Staying positive is not automatic — it requires daily practice and intention.

Why Positivity Matters

Research shows that optimists tend to be healthier and happier than pessimists.

  • They have better physical and mental health.
  • They live longer and experience less stress.
  • Their immune systems work stronger.

Positivity also boosts performance — for example, optimistic salespeople sell more and stay longer in their jobs.

The good news? Anyone can learn to shift toward positive thinking with simple strategies.

Three Ways to Train Your Mind to Stay Positive

1. Separate Fact from Fiction

Negative thoughts grow stronger when we repeat them. Most of them are not facts — they are fear-based assumptions.

  • Pause and write your negative thoughts down.
  • Look for exaggerated words like “always” or “never.”
  • Ask yourself if they are truly true.
  • If needed, check with someone you trust.

Labeling thoughts as just thoughts weakens their power.

2. Identify a Positive

Once you stop the negative cycle, shift your focus to something positive.

  • A small win from today
  • Something you enjoyed recently
  • Something exciting you are looking forward to

Each time negative thinking returns, redirect your attention to this positive anchor.

3. Practice Gratitude

Gratitude reduces stress hormones and increases energy and emotional well-being. Just a few minutes a day can make a difference.

  • Notice what you appreciate — big or small.
  • Let negative thoughts remind you to switch focus.
  • Over time, gratitude becomes a natural habit.

Putting It All Together

These steps sound simple, but they are powerful because they retrain your brain. With practice, a positive mindset becomes easier and more natural.

Even small shifts in attention can change how you feel and live.
author: Travis Bradberry

title: The amazing benefits of houseplants on your mind and body
header: Your home air may be making you sick — discover how a few plants can quietly fix it.
content:
Why Indoor Plants Make Your Home Healthier and Happier

Walking into a conservatory feels special — warm air, soil fragrance, and humidity that refresh the skin. For those living in colder climates, indoor air can get dry for months. While we can’t recreate a greenhouse at home, adding living plants can make a big difference.

Why Plants Matter Indoors

We spend about 90% of our time inside. This raises concerns about “sick building syndrome,” where indoor air causes headaches, sore throats, and other problems.

Research shows that VOCs — chemicals released from carpets, furniture, computers, and more — contribute to this issue. NASA studies found that indoor plants help remove these toxins, improving air quality and reducing complaints.

Plants may also help lower blood pressure and improve mood. Caring for plants — watering, pruning, grooming — can be relaxing after a long day.

Choosing the Right Plants

Light is the first thing to consider. Your window direction affects which plants will thrive.

Bright Southern Windows

  • Cacti and succulents
  • Fiddle leaf fig
  • Hoyas
  • Snake plants

East or West Windows

  • Philodendrons
  • Ferns
  • Begonias
  • African violets
  • Dieffenbachia
  • Pothos

Northern Windows

Low light — best for foliage plants.

  • Aspidistra
  • Philodendron
  • Pothos
  • Peace lily (spathiphyllum)
  • ZZ plant

No Natural Light? You Have Options

If your space lacks windows, grow plants under electric lights. With the right lighting, any plant can thrive — even in a closet or basement.

The Benefits Are Worth It

Indoor plants may:

  • Clean the air
  • Increase humidity
  • Lower blood pressure
  • Boost mood and well-being

A little greenery can make your home healthier and happier — a simple gift from nature.
author: Lisa Eldred Steinkopf

title: Giving Something Back To The Communities You Care About
header: Your everyday talents could be someone else’s breakthrough — explore the power of giving back.
content:
Skills-Based Volunteering: Using What You Know to Help Others

When we hear “volunteering,” we often picture picking up litter or serving meals. But there is another growing form — skills-based volunteering (SBV). This means helping others by sharing skills you already have and enjoy using.

Whether you’re a student, a seasoned professional, or someone with a hobby, your abilities can benefit someone else. You just need to take the first step.

Becoming a Business Mentor

If you work in a professional field, your experience — strategy, decision making, marketing, or people management — can guide someone launching their own business.

  • Meet regularly with a new entrepreneur.
  • Help them grow their ideas and confidence.
  • Share your network to open opportunities.
  • Be a sounding board for challenges and ideas.

Your everyday skills could be life-changing for someone starting out.

Volunteering to Learn Life Skills

Some programs encourage people to volunteer at least 16 hours. In return, volunteers gain access to workshops, life-skill training, and job opportunities.

Companies like Starbucks, Bloomberg, Zendesk and others support these projects — even offering guaranteed interviews to participants. Helping others becomes a pathway for personal growth.

Use Unique Skills — Even Diving

Maybe your skill isn’t office-based — maybe it’s diving. On one island between Ireland and the U.K., local divers formed a group to train community members after a tragic accident.

Their hobby became a tool for saving lives — another example of how skills can support a community.

Inspire Others by Being You

Many talents you take for granted could benefit someone else. Pause and reflect on skills from work, hobbies, or everyday life — you may discover ways to contribute, connect with new people, and even learn something new yourself.

Sometimes the best way to give is simply by being who you are.
author: Emma Galic

title: Tips to Keep Up With Your Sustainable Resolutions
header: Feeling your New Year motivation fading? Try these science-backed ways to stay on track.”
content:
How to Stay Motivated With Your Sustainability Goals

New year, new resolutions — but motivation often fades fast. Don’t worry! Here are simple, powerful ways to keep your sustainable living goals on track.

1. Use the Buddy System

Find a friend or family member who shares similar goals. Working together boosts accountability and motivation.

  • Research shows people who share weekly progress updates are far more likely to reach their goals.
  • Plan realistic steps you both can follow throughout the year.
  • Track progress, encourage each other, and step in when someone slips.

2. Shape Your Environment to Support Your Goals

Your surroundings influence your success. Make your space remind you of your mission.

  • Place posters, notes, or symbols that reinforce your goals.
  • Adjust digital spaces — follow sustainability pages or accounts that inspire you daily.
  • Let small reminders push you forward when motivation dips.

Remember: Small Steps Add Up

Change doesn’t happen overnight. A tiny choice today — like avoiding a takeaway meal — may seem small, but over weeks it saves kilos of plastic.

Consistency beats intensity — keep moving forward, one step at a time.

title: Kindness Makes You Happy and vice versa
header: The more you give, the happier you get — research reveals a powerful loop you’ll want to try.
content:
How Kindness Can Make You Happier

New research suggests that when you start doing kind things for others, you may not want to stop. Helping people doesn’t just feel good in the moment – it can create a lasting happiness loop.

Giving vs. Spending on Yourself

Imagine you could buy happiness in a store. Research shows you get more happiness when what you “buy” is for someone else, not for yourself.

  • Doing kind things for others makes people happier.
  • Spending money on others feels better than spending it on yourself.
  • Kindness can lead to more kindness over time.

Study 1: Acts of Kindness for 10 Days

In one study from the Journal of Social Psychology, 86 people were split into three groups for 10 days:

  • Group 1: Do one kind act every day.
  • Group 2: Do something new every day.
  • Group 3: No special instructions.

What happened?

  • Group 1 (kindness) became happier.
  • Group 2 (novel activities) also became happier.
  • Group 3 did not get happier.

This shows:

  • Kind actions can boost happiness in just 10 days.
  • Doing different kinds of kind acts may help even more.

Study 2: Remembering Giving Makes You Give More

In another study from the Journal of Happiness Studies, 51 people were asked to remember how they spent money in the past.

  • Half remembered a time they spent $20 or $100 on themselves.
  • The other half remembered a time they spent $20 or $100 on someone else.
  • Everyone then rated how happy they felt.

After that, the researchers gave them a small amount of money and a choice:

  • Spend it on themselves (a bill, a personal expense, or a gift for themselves).
  • Spend it on someone else (a donation or a gift for another person).

Their choice was kept anonymous so they didn’t feel judged.

What They Found

  • People felt happier when they remembered giving to others than when they remembered spending on themselves.
  • This was true whether they had given $20 or $100.
  • The happier people felt about their past giving, the more likely they were to give again in the present.

Not everyone felt happy when they remembered giving. But those who did feel happy were much more likely to choose to give again.

A Positive Kindness Loop

The researchers call this a “positive feedback loop” between kindness and happiness:

  • One kind act makes you feel good.
  • Feeling good makes you more likely to be kind again.
  • More kindness leads to more happiness – and the cycle continues.

For example:

  • You take your mom to lunch → you feel happy.
  • Feeling happy makes you more likely to help a friend later.
  • Helping your friend makes you feel good again.

How You Can Use This

  • Do one small kind act each day (a message, a small gift, a favor).
  • Notice how you feel after helping someone.
  • When you feel good about giving, remind yourself of that feeling.
  • Use that feeling to inspire your next kind act.

Charities can also use this idea. If they remind people of their past donations, it may make them feel happy again – and more willing to give.

The Takeaway

Kindness is not just good for others – it’s good for you too. Doing something nice, remembering that kindness, and enjoying the good feeling can keep you giving and growing happier over time.
