title: Good leaders don’t give advice — they coach
header: Why great managers don’t give more advice — they give more autonomy.
content:
Simple Leadership Tips to Help Employees Grow

Great managers guide people — they don’t just tell them what to do. Research shows leaders who coach instead of constantly giving advice help teams learn, grow, and perform better.

Here are three easy Microsteps you can start using today to become a more supportive leader.

1. Start Meetings With a Clear Goal

Help everyone stay focused by opening each meeting with one simple purpose.

  • Say what the meeting is trying to achieve.
  • Let the team work toward that goal together.
  • This builds unity and keeps discussions on track.

2. Pause Before Giving Feedback

Before you jump in with advice, take a moment to check your own mindset.

  • If you’re stressed or rushed, feedback can sound harsh.
  • Take a breath and calm yourself first.
  • This helps you give guidance with clarity and respect.

3. Give Feedback With Compassion

Feedback doesn’t have to be blunt or cold. Make it supportive and direct.

  • Be honest, kind, and clear.
  • Encourage employees to speak up, share concerns, or disagree.
  • This builds trust and a healthier work culture.

Small changes like these make leadership easier and help your team grow with confidence.
author: Ian Burke

title: Reasons Why Wanting To Be Alone Is Good For You
header: Why are we scared of our own thoughts? The surprising truth about being alone.
content:
Why Spending Time Alone Is Good for You

A study showed that many people — especially men — prefer shocking themselves over sitting quietly with their thoughts. But being alone isn’t bad at all. It can actually help you grow.

“Me time” doesn’t mean you are anti-social or unwanted. It simply means you are giving yourself space to recharge.

1. You Grow as a Person

  • Quiet time helps you reset.
  • No need to constantly interact or please others.
  • Your energy goes inward, helping you reflect and improve.

2. You Understand Yourself Better

  • You step away from other people’s drama.
  • You notice your real needs and emotions.
  • You learn what makes you happy or upset.

3. You Do What You Enjoy

  • Your time belongs to you.
  • Eat, sleep, or relax without pressure or judgment.

4. You Become More Productive

  • Fewer distractions mean more focus.
  • Solo time often leads to your best work.

5. You Learn to Prioritize

  • You choose what matters instead of trying to do it all.
  • Focusing on fewer things brings more fulfillment.

Remember: being alone isn’t loneliness. It’s a healthy space to breathe, grow, and enjoy your own company.
author: Shikha Gandhi

title: What we've learned about mental health from young people
header: Why mental health must become a global priority — and what we can do today.
content:
The Global Youth Mental Health Crisis

Mental health affects every country, culture, and generation. The scale of the crisis can feel overwhelming, but it also reminds us why we must understand its causes and support wellbeing in our communities.

Young people are especially vulnerable. In the U.S., one in five teens aged 13–18 live with a mental health condition, and half of all conditions begin by age 14. If left unaddressed, these struggles can continue into adulthood and limit opportunities for a fulfilling life.

Why Mental Health Matters

  • Young people aged 15–24 make up almost 20% of the world’s population.
  • They represent 15% of the global workforce.
  • Mental illness may cost the world $16 trillion by 2030.

When leaders ignore mental health in workplaces and schools, productivity, potential, and overall wellbeing suffer.

The Barriers Young People Face

  • Many care about their mental health but don’t talk about it.
  • Half say they don’t know where to find support.
  • Cost is a major barrier—many cannot afford help.
  • Mental health receives less than 1% of global aid.

These facts show we need better education, access, and solutions.

How We Can Help

  • Create simple digital tools that make finding help easy.
  • Train community members to support one another.
  • Raise awareness and start open conversations.

Young people are already taking action—building campaigns, sharing resources, and encouraging dialogue.

The Good News

  • Workplaces are improving mental health benefits.
  • Governments are dedicating more resources.
  • The United Nations has included mental health in its goals.

Now is the time to move faster, learn from one another, and close the gap between youth and the support they need.
author: Cynthia Germanotta & Maya Smith

title: Steps to Happiness
header: Research says these small actions can make you happier — and you’re probably skipping them.
content:
Simple Ways to Boost Your Happiness

Here are easy, beginner-friendly habits you can try to improve your wellbeing.

1. Learn to Forgive

  • Write in a journal about letting go of anger or hurt.
  • Try drafting a letter (you don’t need to send it).

2. Practice Acts of Kindness

  • Do small good deeds — planned or spontaneous.
  • Help a friend or even a stranger.

3. Nurture Relationships

  • Choose one relationship to improve.
  • Spend time, listen, or show appreciation.

4. Cultivate Optimism

  • Keep a journal imagining your best future.
  • Look for the bright side in daily moments.

5. Avoid Over-Thinking and Comparison

  • Use distraction when your thoughts get stuck.
  • Notice when you compare yourself to others and pause.

6. Build Coping Skills

  • Practice ways to handle stress or challenges.
  • Try breathing, talking to someone, or problem-solving.

7. Count Your Blessings

  • Write down what you are grateful for.
  • Thank someone you’ve never properly thanked.

8. Strengthen Spiritual Connections

  • Join a group or community that lifts you up.
  • Connect through reflection, prayer, or meaning-making.

9. Commit to Your Goals

  • Pick 1–3 meaningful goals.
  • Spend a little time toward them each week.

10. Take Care of Your Body

  • Move your body — walk, stretch, or exercise.
  • Smile, laugh, or meditate to relax your mind.

title: Does Mind-Wandering Make You Unhappy?
header: Want to feel happier? Start by understanding this surprising mental habit.
content:
What Really Makes Us Happy?

Big life events like money, education, or marriage do matter — but research shows they only make small differences. What matters more is what we experience from moment to moment.

Happiness in Daily Life

  • What you are doing
  • Who you are with
  • What you are thinking about

These everyday moments have a stronger effect on happiness than big life milestones.

A Study on Real-Time Happiness

Researchers created trackyourhappiness.org to send people quick questions throughout the day using their phones. Over 15,000 people replied, offering more than 650,000 moment-by-moment reports.

They answered three simple questions:

  • How happy do you feel right now?
  • What are you doing? (work, eating, relaxing, etc.)
  • Is your mind on the present moment or somewhere else?

The Big Discovery: Mind-Wandering

On average, people are thinking about something else almost 47% of the time.

Examples:

  • 65% mind-wandering while showering
  • 50% while working
  • 40% while exercising
  • 10% during intimacy

Mind-wandering is not rare — it happens almost everywhere.

Mind-Wandering and Unhappiness

The study found:

  • People are less happy when their mind wanders.
  • This is true even during boring tasks like commuting.
  • Mind-wandering often leads to thinking about worries and regrets.

Even when wandering toward pleasant thoughts, people were still slightly less happy than when fully present.

Does Unhappiness Cause Mind-Wandering?

No — the study suggests the opposite.

  • Mind-wandering comes first.
  • Unhappiness often follows.

This means drifting away from the present moment can be a major reason for feeling less happy.

The Simple Lesson

You don’t need to stop thinking or planning — but learning to be more present can make daily life feel richer and calmer.

Try These Small Practices

  • Focus on one task at a time
  • Notice when your mind drifts — gently return to now
  • Pay attention to small moments like eating or walking

Happiness grows when we are engaged in the moment — not lost somewhere else.
author: MATT KILLINGSWORTH

title: Reasons why reading books is good for you
header: Discover why physical books might help you remember more.
content:
Why Reading Is Good for You

Reading isn’t just enjoyable — research shows it brings real benefits. Here are five simple reasons to pick up a book today.

1. Reading Can Help You Live Longer

  • Studies show book readers live about two years longer than non-readers.
  • Books give a stronger survival benefit than newspapers or magazines.
  • Deep reading builds empathy and emotional intelligence — skills linked to well-being.

2. You Learn Better from Physical Books

  • Research shows students remember more from paper than screens.
  • Printed books may support better focus and comprehension.

3. Reading Builds Future-Ready Skills

  • Growing up with books improves literacy, problem-solving, and numeracy.
  • These skills are becoming more important in today’s changing world.

4. It Expands Your Vocabulary

  • Readers develop stronger vocabulary growth than non-readers.
  • Reading aloud and talking about books helps children learn new words.

5. It Protects Your Brain

  • Reading and other mental challenges may reduce your risk of dementia.
  • The brain stays healthier when we keep using it — “use it or lose it.”

Many global book clubs even let you join discussions and talk with authors online.

So why wait? Grab a good book and enjoy reading today.
author: Emma Charlton

title: Those who drink tea regularly have healthier brains, research shows
header: New study: long-term tea drinkers show stronger, more efficient brain networks.
content:
Tea and Brain Health

New research shows that people who drink tea regularly have better organized brain networks — linked to healthier thinking and memory — compared to those who don’t.

Scientists found that drinking green, oolong, or black tea at least four times a week for about 25 years may help protect the brain from age-related decline.

Key Findings

  • Regular tea drinkers showed stronger and more efficient brain connections.
  • Better brain organization supports smoother information processing.
  • Previous studies show tea drinkers had sharper cognitive function.
  • One study suggested tea could cut cognitive decline risk by 50%.

How It Works

  • Researchers compared MRI scans and thinking tests of adults aged 60+.
  • Tea seems to help keep communication pathways in the brain intact.
  • This supports memory, focus, and mental efficiency.

Scientists plan to continue studying tea’s active compounds to see how they protect the brain as we age.

Simple takeaway: A regular cup of tea may do more than refresh you — it may support long-term brain health.
author: National University of Singapore

title: How Awe Makes Us Generous
header: The Strange Reason Feeling Small in Nature Makes You Kinder — New Research Reveals Why
content:
Awe Can Make Us Kinder

A new study shows that feeling small in nature — like staring at stars or standing before a huge canyon — can inspire kindness and generosity.

Researchers found that awe doesn’t just feel good personally — it encourages us to help others.

What is Awe?

  • A deep sense of wonder.
  • Feeling connected to something bigger than yourself.
  • A reminder that we are part of a much larger world.

Key Study Findings

  • People who often feel awe tend to act more generously.
  • Remembering an awe moment (like a sunrise) increases ethical behavior.
  • Watching awe-filled videos leads to more kindness than funny or neutral videos.

Experiments in Real Life

  • Students who stared at tall trees helped more when someone dropped pens.
  • Even awe from disaster footage or close-up water droplets encouraged fairness.

Why It Works

Awe gives people a “small self” feeling — less focus on ego and more focus on others.

Awe Spreads

People who feel awe want to share it — suggesting awe can ripple through communities.

Simple takeaway: Look up at trees, stars, mountains, or art — those moments may make you more generous and connected to others.

title: Why water makes us feel better, according to science
header: Scientists Found Why Water Sparks Awe, Creativity, and Peace — Dive In to Learn More
content:
Blue Mind: Why Water Helps Us Feel Calm and Happy

Feeling stressed or overwhelmed? Science says water might be a natural healer — and you don’t need to live at the beach to feel its benefits.

Why Water Helps

  • Water environments (sea, lakes, rivers, fountains, showers) help us relax.
  • Simply hearing water or looking at water scenes can calm the brain.
  • Our bodies and brains are mostly water — so we naturally respond to it.

Scientists call this “blue mind” — a calm, peaceful state triggered by water.

Key Benefits of Blue Mind

  • Makes us happier and calmer.
  • Boosts creativity and problem-solving.
  • Improves mood and lowers stress.
  • Helps us feel small in a meaningful way — more humble, more connected.

Red Mind vs Blue Mind

  • Red mind: Stress from city life, screens, and constant notifications.
  • Blue mind: Peaceful state supported by water and nature.

Spending time near water — or even looking at water images — can shift us from red to blue.

No Ocean? No Problem.

You can experience blue mind anywhere:

  • Take a long shower — like a mini vacation for your brain.
  • Listen to flowing water sounds.
  • Watch nature videos with rivers or oceans.
  • Visit fountains, canals, or lakes in city spaces.

Awe Makes Us Kinder

Water often inspires awe — a feeling of wonder and perspective.

  • Awe reduces ego.
  • Helps us see the bigger picture.
  • Makes us more generous and caring toward others.

So whenever you feel overwhelmed, stop — breathe — and find some water. Even a shower or a stream sound can refresh your mind.
author: Ephrat Livni

title: Giving Is Good
header: “The Hidden Benefits of Generosity: Why Giving Makes You Happier, Healthier, and More Connected
content:
Why Giving Makes Us Happier and Healthier

New research shows that giving — whether money, time, or kindness — benefits not only others but also the giver.

1. Giving Makes Us Happier

  • People felt happier giving to others than spending on themselves.
  • Acts of kindness trigger a “helper’s high” — a warm, positive feeling.
  • Giving activates brain areas linked to pleasure and connection.

2. Giving Is Good for Our Health

  • Generosity is linked to better physical health, even in older adults.
  • Elderly volunteers lived longer than non-volunteers.
  • Helping others reduces stress and lowers blood pressure.

3. Giving Builds Cooperation and Connection

  • Kindness increases trust and strengthens communities.
  • Giving often leads to receiving help later — sometimes from unexpected people.
  • Being generous helps us feel closer to others.

4. Giving Creates Gratitude

  • Giving and receiving gifts both inspire gratitude.
  • Gratitude boosts happiness, optimism, and well-being.
  • Expressing thanks strengthens relationships.

5. Giving Is Contagious

  • One act of generosity inspires others to pay it forward.
  • Kindness can ripple through communities — from person to person.
  • Giving may release oxytocin, boosting empathy and connection.

So whether you donate, volunteer, or simply help someone, giving is more than a good deed — it strengthens happiness, health, and whole communities.

title: Ways To Pursue Happiness
header: Science Says Happiness Isn’t a Mystery — Discover the Daily Habits That Quietly Transform Your Life
content:
Simple Ways to Feel Happier Every Day

Happiness is not a mystery. Small, daily habits can make life brighter. Even a fun activity like a photo session can lift mood and confidence. Here are easy ways to pursue happiness.

Practice Gratitude

Gratitude means noticing and appreciating the good things in your life.

  • Keep a small gratitude journal.
  • Spend 10–15 minutes daily writing things you are thankful for.
  • Gratitude increases happiness and emotional balance.

Do Things You Enjoy

People often forget to spend time on activities they love.

  • Think about what you enjoyed last week.
  • If you didn’t do much for yourself, add it to your schedule.
  • Choose hobbies, sports, or quality time with loved ones.

Learn to Love Your Job

You spend a big part of life working. Enjoying your job boosts happiness.

  • Reconnect with what motivates you.
  • Practice gratitude at work.
  • Get involved and build positive workplace connections.

Celebrate Small Wins

We often focus on problems and forget to celebrate good moments.

  • Notice small successes or happy events.
  • Celebrate relationships and personal achievements.
  • Pause to appreciate progress — not just big milestones.

Build Self-Confidence

Low confidence affects happiness. Train your mind to think positively.

  • Write qualities you like about yourself.
  • Visualize your best self.
  • Replace negative self-talk with encouraging thoughts.

Dream Big

Many people stop themselves from trying because they think big dreams are impossible.

  • Believe that change is possible.
  • Break your dream into small goals.
  • Take the first step — big results start small.

Happiness grows when you practice these small habits. Start today — your brighter life is in your hands.
author: Naina

title: A new study may have revealed a key reason for poor sleep
header: Scientists Just Found the Hidden Brain Link Between Depression and Sleepless Nights — Explore What It Means for You
content:
Depression and Sleep: What New Research Reveals

Scientists have discovered a brain link that explains why depression and sleep problems often occur together.

They found that certain brain areas — linked to memory, self-thinking, and negative emotions — connect more strongly in people with depression. This over-connection leads to negative thoughts that make it harder to sleep well.

Why This Matters

This insight may help improve sleep for people with depression and guide new treatments in the future.

Key Findings

  • About 75% of people with depression struggle with sleep problems.
  • People with insomnia have a higher risk of depression and anxiety.
  • Researchers studied data from nearly 10,000 people.

Brain Areas Involved

  • Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex: linked to short-term memory.
  • Precuneus: linked to the sense of self.
  • Lateral orbitofrontal cortex: linked to negative emotions.

These areas show high activity together in depressed individuals. This creates more rumination — repeated negative thinking — which harms sleep quality.

Why It’s Important

Researchers believe this brain connection explains why depression and poor sleep are strongly linked.

They also suggest that the orbitofrontal cortex could become a target for new depression treatments.

A Growing Global Problem

  • Insomnia affects more than one-third of the world.
  • Depression affects about 216 million people worldwide.
  • Most people are either affected themselves or know someone who is.

The hope is that understanding these brain patterns will lead to better support and healthier sleep for millions.
author: Luke Walton

title: Relationship Tips To Build A Stronger Bond And Happier Futures
header: Want a Stronger, Happier Relationship? These Daily Micro-Habits Could Change Everything
content:
7 Simple Ways to Build a Stronger Relationship

You don’t need expensive gifts or big trips to make your partner happy. Small daily actions help create a deeper bond.

Here are seven easy tips for a healthier and happier relationship.

1. Argue to Fix, Not to Win

  • Focus on solving the problem.
  • Avoid bringing up old issues.
  • Speak kindly, not to hurt.
  • Try to understand your partner’s point of view.

2. Communicate Regularly

  • Talk often, even about simple daily things.
  • Share thoughts and feelings.
  • Good communication reduces stress and prevents conflict.

3. Laugh Together

  • Laughing improves mood and lowers stress.
  • Inside jokes help couples feel closer.
  • Humor can calm tension during disagreements.

4. Say "I Love You"

  • Say it sincerely, not out of routine.
  • Show love with hugs, kisses, or kind messages.
  • Small gestures create closeness.

5. Learn What Your Partner Values

People feel loved in different ways:

  • Words of affirmation
  • Quality time
  • Acts of service
  • Physical touch
  • Receiving gifts

Knowing what matters to your partner helps you love them better.

6. Go to Bed Together

  • Shared bedtime increases connection.
  • Touch boosts the “love hormone” oxytocin.
  • Couples who end the day together feel closer.

7. Be Honest

  • Trust is the foundation of a strong relationship.
  • Be truthful and faithful in action and words.
  • Honesty helps you communicate better and solve problems.

Strong relationships grow through effort, love, and small daily habits. Practice these tips to build a happier future together.
author: Sylvia Smith

title: Happiness is about Respect, not Riches
header: Want to Be Happier? Researchers Say You’re Looking in the Wrong Place — Here’s Where to Look Instead
content:
Respect Makes Us Happier Than Money

New research shows that money does not guarantee happiness. What really matters is how respected and valued we feel by people around us.

Scientists call this sociometric status — the level of admiration and recognition we receive in our social circles.

What The Study Found

  • People who feel respected and admired by friends or colleagues are happier.
  • Income and wealth did not strongly predict happiness.
  • Feeling accepted, valued, and powerful in a group made people feel better.

How The Research Worked

Researchers ran several experiments:

  • Students rated how admired they felt and how happy they were.
  • Adults did the same for their work, family, and friend groups.
  • People were made to imagine having high or low status — only higher social respect increased happiness.
  • MBA graduates were tracked for nine months — changes in social respect affected their happiness more than income changes.

What Makes Us Feel Happy?

According to the study, happiness grows when we feel:

  • Respected for who we are
  • Accepted in our groups
  • Trusted and valued
  • Able to influence or help others

How To Build This Kind of Happiness

You don’t have to be rich. You just need to be a positive member of your community.

  • Be engaged and involved.
  • Be generous with your time and support.
  • Make sacrifices for the greater good.
  • Help others feel valued.

The study reminds us that real happiness comes from belonging, contribution, and respect — not wealth.
author: STACEY KENNELLY

title: Is a Happy Life Different from a Meaningful One?
header: The Secret Link Between Purpose and Happiness Scientists Are Arguing About Right Now
content:
Meaning vs Happiness — What Truly Matters?

People have long debated what makes life worth living. Is it pleasure and comfort, or purpose and meaning? New research helps explain how the two are similar — and different.

Happiness vs Meaning: Key Differences

Researchers found five major ways the two differ:

  • Happiness satisfies needs — meaning does not depend on comfort or wealth.
  • Happiness focuses on now — meaning connects past, present, and future.
  • Meaning comes from giving — happiness often comes from receiving.
  • Meaning includes stress — purpose often brings challenges and sacrifice.
  • Self-expression matters for meaning — identity and creativity fuel purpose.

Example: parenting brings purpose, but can also bring stress — meaning grows even if happiness in the moment drops.

Why So Much Debate?

Researchers disagree because “happiness” can mean different things:

  • Short-term good feelings
  • Life satisfaction
  • Deep fulfillment

Some say you cannot separate meaning from happiness — because joy often comes from meaningful actions.

Eudaimonic vs Hedonic Happiness

  • Hedonic happiness = pleasure, comfort, enjoyment.
  • Eudaimonic happiness = purpose, growth, contribution.

Studies show meaning-driven happiness improves health, mood, and resilience — possibly more than pleasure-only lifestyles.

Do We Need Both?

Yes. Research suggests:

  • Meaning increases happiness.
  • Happiness can help us find meaning.
  • The two feed each other.

So How Do We Live Well?

  • Invest in deep relationships.
  • Give to others.
  • Express your true self.
  • Work toward long-term goals.
  • Look beyond personal comfort.

Pursuing meaning doesn’t block happiness — it often creates it. When you aim for purpose, pleasure and joy tend to follow.
author: JILL SUTTIE, JASON MARSH

title: Sense of humor is an essential life skill
header: Discover the Secret Power of Humor — Your Brain and Body Will Thank You
content:
The Power of Humor — Why It Matters

Humor isn’t just entertainment — studies show it helps your mind, body, relationships, and even leadership skills.

What Is Humor?

Psychologists explain humor through three main ideas:

  • Relief theory: Humor releases emotional pressure — which is why people laugh even during sad moments.
  • Superiority theory: Some jokes make us feel “above” others — but this style isn’t great for healthy relationships.
  • Incongruity theory: Humor works when something unexpected or surprising flips our usual thinking.

How Humor Helps Us

A good sense of humor acts like an emotional immune system:

  • Helps protect against stress and depression.
  • Boosts confidence and positive mood.
  • Improves social connection and communication.
  • Supports immune function, heart health, and relaxation.
  • Enhances creativity, problem-solving, and productivity.

Different Styles of Humor

Researchers identify four types:

  • Affiliative humor – bonding and making others feel good ✔
  • Self-enhancing humor – finding joy in life ✔
  • Aggressive humor – mocking or putting others down ✘
  • Self-defeating humor – belittling yourself for approval ✘

The healthiest kinds are affiliative and self-enhancing — they build resilience and wellbeing.

Can Humor Be Learned?

Yes — experts believe humor can grow with practice.

  • Everyone has some natural capacity for humor.
  • Understanding how humor works helps you use it better.
  • Schools like Stanford now teach humor as a leadership skill.

Even if genetics play a role, you can improve by:

  • Noticing the funny side of everyday life.
  • Practicing light, kind humor with others.
  • Letting yourself laugh more often.

Worst case? You smile a little more. Best case? Humor becomes one of your greatest strengths.
author: Matt Davis

title: Loneliness has become a global epidemic among young people today
header: The Surprising Ways Loneliness Warps Your Thinking (And Hurts Your Health)
content:
Loneliness in Young People — What We Learned

New research shows more than one in three young adults (18–25) report high levels of loneliness. This affects mood, confidence, and mental health.

Key Findings

  • 1 in 4 young people felt lonely on 3+ days within the last week.
  • For ages 18–25, this rises to 35%.
  • Loneliness increases risk of depression (12%) and social anxiety (10%).
  • Younger teens (12–17) reported fewer loneliness symptoms.

Why Young Adults Feel Lonely

  • Moving away from home or starting work/studies.
  • Changing friendships and new environments.
  • Needing to build new relationships and social skills.

Is Social Media the Cause?

Social media can help or harm — but research is unclear on whether it directly causes loneliness.

  • Lonely people often use the internet more.
  • Online interactions can replace or strengthen real connections.
  • Studies show the link between social media and distress is weak.

Loneliness and Mental Health

  • Loneliness can increase depression, anxiety, and paranoia.
  • Social anxiety can increase loneliness later.
  • Lonely people may find social interactions stressful.

Research shows lonely people often:

  • Expect rejection.
  • Feel less rewarded in social settings.
  • Withdraw or act defensively without realising it.

How We Can Help

Support should teach young people how friendship and behaviour influence connection.

Helpful Strategies

  • Challenge negative thoughts about others.
  • Help young people recognise their strengths.
  • Guide them on how to use these strengths to connect (e.g., humour or kindness).
  • Teach relationship-building skills in schools.

Using Technology to Support Young People

  • Safe digital tools can help build social confidence.
  • Apps can teach emotional skills and connection habits.

Normalize Loneliness

Feeling lonely is not weakness — it is a human need for connection.

Talking about loneliness and understanding it reduces shame and encourages action.

The Takeaway

We don’t yet know the long-term effects of loneliness on today’s youth.

But we can act now by raising awareness, offering support, and helping young people build strong, healthy relationships.
author: Michelle Lim

title: what passionate people do differently?
header: What Passionate People Do Differently — And Why It Changes Everything. Explore the science.
content:
What Passion Really Looks Like

Passion is more than a hobby — it defines who you are. It gives you energy, focus, and the excitement to jump out of bed each morning.

Researcher Dr. Robert Vallerand says passion is a strong love for an activity you see as part of your identity, and something you willingly invest time and effort into.

“Passion is the genesis of genius.” — Galileo

You don’t need to be an expert to be passionate, but passion often pushes you toward mastery because you want to become your best self.

How Passionate People Stand Out

1. They are obsessed — in a good way

Their mind naturally returns to their passion, not from pressure but excitement and joy.

2. They value their time

They don’t waste hours on things that don’t matter. Free time goes into what fuels them most.

3. They are optimistic

They always look ahead, believing progress and success are possible.

4. They wake up eager

Passionate people rise early — not because they dislike sleep, but because their purpose pulls them forward.

5. They take risks

When you deeply care about something, you are willing to bet on it and face uncertainty.

6. They go “all in”

They operate at full effort or full rest — nothing halfway.

7. They talk about their passion often

Because their passion is who they are, it naturally shows up in conversations.

8. They get excited easily

Progress sparks momentum. Even small wins keep them motivated.

9. Their work is part of their identity

They don’t separate “work” and “life.” To them, their work is life — and they love it.

Final Thought

Passion fuels purpose, effort, and happiness. Now that you know the traits — ask yourself: how much passion is shaping your life?
author: Travis Bradberry

title: Why It Is So Important To Dream That Dream And Never Give Up
header: Giving Up Would’ve Been Easier—But She Chose a Lesson Her Kids Will Carry Forever
content:
Keep Creating — Someone Is Watching

Art gives us a sense of accomplishment, even if no one ever sees the work. For many, creating is part of who we are. But we also dream that one day our creations will be noticed — maybe even enough to leave the day job behind.

I once chased that dream in every spare moment. But life was happening beside me. I had two children, then later a third, and I found myself living in two worlds — parenthood and creative ambition.

When my youngest was born, I paused and reflected. Should I give up? Instead, I realized my children were the reason I had to keep going.

My teenagers already knew about my dreams. What message would giving up send to them? And what would their baby sister learn if I stopped trying?

Sometimes our efforts slow down — children and responsibilities require attention. But they don’t have to end. Living your dream is part of teaching them to live theirs.

Even if I never “make it big,” I will know I never quit. That lesson — persistence — is what I want my children to see.

Final Thought

Keep going. Someone is watching, learning, and drawing strength from your example.
author: Rebecca

title: Why true happiness isn’t about being happy all the time
header: You Don’t Need to Be Happy All the Time—Science Says Something Much Better Matters
content:
The Science of Happiness (In Simple Words)

Happiness is not just about always smiling or feeling good. Modern psychology says it is about:

  • Feeling positive emotions often (joy, calm, excitement)
  • Living with meaning and purpose
  • Having hope for the future

Positive psychology, led by researcher Martin Seligman, studies not only problems and illness but also what makes life feel worth living.

Happiness Is Flexible, Not Fixed

Happiness is not something you are born with and stuck with. It can change.

  • We can learn skills to think and feel in healthier ways.
  • We can build habits that support long-term happiness.
  • We can grow even when life is hard.

Researchers call this psychological flexibility. It means:

  • Being open to all emotions (good and bad)
  • Accepting that discomfort is part of life
  • Still moving towards what matters to you

You Don’t Need To Be Happy All The Time

Feeling stress, sadness, or anxiety does not mean you have a “bad life.”

  • Everyone has difficult days.
  • Short-term pain does not cancel long-term happiness.
  • How you respond matters more than what happens.

Studies show that our response to events affects our happiness more than the events themselves.

Two Different Paths To Happiness

Philosophers talk about two main types of happiness:

1. Hedonic Happiness

  • Focus: Pleasure and comfort
  • Goal: Get more fun, avoid pain
  • Example: Eating tasty food, relaxing, buying something nice
  • Problem: The good feeling often fades quickly, so we always want more

2. Eudaimonic Happiness

  • Focus: Meaning, growth, and living your values
  • Goal: Be honest, kind, brave, and useful to others
  • Example: Helping someone, learning, doing the right thing even when it is hard
  • Result: Deeper joy and long-lasting contentment

If we only chase pleasure (hedonic), we may:

  • Keep needing new highs
  • Try to avoid any pain
  • Feel empty when excitement is gone

If we focus on meaning (eudaimonic), we may:

  • Face hard emotions sometimes
  • Do difficult but important things
  • Feel more proud, grounded, and fulfilled

How Hard Times Can Help Us Grow

Struggles can sometimes make our lives richer in the long run — if we learn and grow from them.

  • Facing problems can build courage and resilience.
  • Pain can push us to make positive changes (like changing jobs or habits).
  • We may discover what truly matters to us.

Researchers call this post-traumatic growth. Many people say that after illness, loss, or trauma, they:

  • Appreciate life more deeply
  • Value relationships more
  • Feel stronger and more purposeful

Happiness vs. A Happy Life

Feeling happy is a short-term emotion. It comes and goes.

Leading a happy life is bigger. It means:

  • Growing as a person
  • Finding meaning in what you do
  • Accepting both good and bad days
  • Using both joy and pain to move toward your full potential

Key Takeaways

  • You don’t need to be happy all the time to have a good life.
  • Happiness is flexible — you can build it with habits and choices.
  • Chasing only pleasure is not enough.
  • Meaning, growth, and values create deeper, lasting happiness.
  • Hard times can help you grow if you let them teach you.

A good life is not about avoiding every storm — it is about learning, growing, and finding meaning as you walk through them.
author: Lowri Dowthwaite

title: This is how you can find meaning in your life, and still be happy
header: Are You Living a Happy Life… or a Meaningful One? Science Says You Can’t Always Have Both.
content:
Finding Balance: Happiness and Meaning

Many things can make us feel happy, like:

  • A relaxing hot shower
  • Watching funny shows
  • Eating our favourite treats
  • Wearing something that looks good

But sometimes these moments feel good without giving life deeper purpose.

On the other hand, some meaningful acts do not feel happy at all, such as:

  • Caring for an elderly parent
  • Working hard to support children
  • Sacrificing comfort to fight injustice
  • Helping others at personal cost

These examples show two realities:

  • Happy moments can lack meaning.
  • Meaningful acts can feel difficult and painful.

Two Ways of Living

Some people choose pleasure first (“hedonists”). Others choose duty and meaning (“stoics”).

But a richer life usually needs both.

How Can We Have Both?

Sometimes we can take turns — for example:

  • A nurse faces stress and suffering during work
  • Later, they relax, dance, or enjoy a quiet evening

Another way is to find activities that give:

  • Meaning through effort
  • Happiness through enjoyment

What Do These Activities Look Like?

Examples include:

  • Growing a flower garden for family
  • Writing or sharing ideas that help others
  • Inventing something useful
  • Improving your health through exercise
  • Caring for a pet
  • Learning to play music
  • Having meaningful talks with children
  • Helping people work well together

These moments feel good, and they matter.

The Sweet Spot

You don’t need to stop enjoying simple pleasures. You also don’t need to give up meaningful work.

The goal is to spend more time where happiness and meaning meet — doing things that feel good and make life richer.

Live in that sweet spot whenever you can.
author: Thaddeus Metz

title: Secrets to happiness, according to Roman Stoics
header: Why Ancient Roman Wisdom Might Be the Mental Health Tool You Actually Need Today
content:
Simple Stoic Lessons for Modern Life

The ancient Romans are known for roads and buildings — but they also left guidance for living well. Three key Stoic thinkers were:

  • Seneca (advisor to Nero)
  • Epictetus (a former slave)
  • Marcus Aurelius (a Roman emperor)

Today, their ideas are popular again through books and courses on how to live calmly and wisely.

What Stoicism Teaches

Stoicism says a good life starts with a good mindset. It means:

  • Living with reason and virtue
  • Staying calm during challenges
  • Accepting what we cannot control

1. Focus on What You Can Control

Epictetus taught that:

  • We cannot control events
  • We cannot control other people
  • We cannot fully control our bodies
  • The one thing we control is how we think about things

We create stress when we try to control things outside our control. Peace begins when we manage our reactions instead.

2. Change Your Judgements, Change Your Emotions

Stoics say:

  • Events are neutral
  • We give them meaning by our thoughts
  • Emotion comes from judgement, not the event itself

So if we adjust our thinking, we can reduce anger, fear, and sadness.

3. Train Your Mind Daily

Stoicism is not just theory — it requires practice. Examples include:

  • Review your day each night — where did you react badly?
  • Plan ahead for annoying people or difficult moments
  • Remind yourself that others act from mistaken thinking, not intention

This training helps us respond better instead of reacting automatically.

4. Accept What Happens

Marcus Aurelius reflected daily on:

  • How small his life is compared to time and space
  • How little the world owes us

Stoics teach:

  • Stop expecting life to match your wishes
  • Accept events calmly instead of fighting them

If you stop demanding life to be your way, life becomes smoother.

Final Thought

Stoicism is not about ignoring feelings — it is about:

  • Choosing better thoughts
  • Practicing calmer reactions
  • Living with acceptance and wisdom

These ancient lessons still help people today live more peaceful, strong, and meaningful lives.
author: John Sellars

title: Ways to increase your emotional intelligence
header: The Powerful Things Emotionally Smart People Avoid — Most People Never Notice
content:
9 Things Emotionally Smart People Avoid

Managing emotions is not only about what you do — it’s also about what you avoid doing. Here are nine habits emotionally intelligent people stay away from.

1. They Don’t Let Others Control Their Joy

They don’t compare themselves to others. Their value comes from within, not from people’s opinions.

  • They celebrate their progress
  • They don’t let criticism ruin their mood

2. They Forgive but Don’t Forget

They let go of hurt but protect themselves from repeat harm.

  • They move on quickly
  • They learn from mistakes

3. They Don’t Fight Every Battle

They choose their battles wisely and avoid conflicts that drain their energy.

4. They Don’t Chase Perfection

They aim for progress, not perfection. They know perfection is impossible.

  • They celebrate wins
  • They focus on growth, not flaws

5. They Don’t Live in the Past

They learn from setbacks but stay focused on the future.

6. They Don’t Dwell on Problems

They look for solutions instead of complaining.

  • Problems = stress
  • Solutions = confidence and progress

7. They Avoid Negative Company

They set boundaries with people who complain without solving anything.

  • They don’t join pity parties
  • They ask, “How will you fix it?” to redirect the talk

8. They Don’t Hold Grudges

Grudges create stress and hurt your health. Emotionally smart people let go.

  • Letting go = peace
  • Grudges = stress and poor health

9. They Don’t Say Yes When They Mean No

They protect their time and energy by saying “no” clearly and confidently.

  • They honor their current commitments
  • They avoid burnout

Small changes in what you avoid can boost your emotional strength, confidence, and performance.

title: Why the key to living longer might be to stop worrying about it
header: Your Mindset Could Be Secretly Impacting Your Lifespan — Discover Why It Matters More Than Stress Itself
content:
Mindset Matters: How You Think Affects Your Health

Research shows something surprising — your beliefs about your activity level or stress can affect your health as much as the activity or stress itself.

Exercise Mindset

A study of 60,000+ adults found:

  • People who believed they were less active were up to 71% more likely to die earlier — even if they exercised.
  • Believing you move enough can improve health.

Example: Hotel workers told their job counted as exercise showed:

  • Lower blood pressure
  • Weight loss
  • Better waist-to-hip ratio
  • Improved BMI

Belief changed their bodies — without changing their routines.

Stress Mindset

Stress itself isn’t always harmful.

  • People with high stress but who didn’t believe it was harmful had the lowest death risk.
  • People who believed stress was dangerous and felt stressed had a 43% higher death risk.

Your view of stress can harm you more than stress itself.

How to Shift Your Mindset

1. Stop Comparing

Don’t measure your activity against others or social media standards.

2. Celebrate What You Do

  • Praise yourself for movement
  • Don’t punish yourself for missed workouts

3. Don’t Fear Stress

  • Stress is normal
  • It is part of survival, not always danger

4. See Stress as Helpful

Viewing stress as a tool can improve outcomes.

Final Thought

Your mindset can lift your health — changing worry into acceptance may be one of the healthiest habits you can build.
author: Robin Bailey

title: Happy employees are more productive, research shows
header: Feeling Happy Today? Science Says You’ll Work Faster and Sell More — Discover the Surprising Data
content:
Happy Employees Work Better

How you feel today matters more than you think. New research shows that happy employees are more productive at work.

What the Study Found

Researchers from Oxford University studied 1,800 call centre workers over six months.

  • Each worker rated their happiness weekly using simple emoji buttons.
  • Happier workers made more calls per hour.
  • They achieved 13% higher sales than unhappy workers.
  • They didn’t work extra hours — they just used time better.

Why It Matters

Paid work isn’t always fun, so employers must try harder to support employee wellbeing.

Improving happiness:

  • Boosts productivity
  • Benefits workers and companies

What Affects Happiness?

Some things can lower happiness that we can’t control:

  • Bad weather — rain, fog, and snow make people feel gloomy.

Interestingly:

  • Weather did not increase sick days.

Do Happy People Perform Better?

The study suggests that workers bring their happiness to work — not the other way around.

  • Happy employees perform better because they already feel good.
  • This effect is strongest in customer-facing jobs.
  • Happiness improves social skills, leading to happier customers and more sales.

What’s Next for Work?

Experts suggest employers should:

  • Rethink hiring and motivation
  • Invest in reskilling employees
  • Focus on human skills in a tech-driven world

Final Thought

Happiness isn’t just good for people — it’s good for business. Supporting wellbeing can lead to better results for everyone.
author: Douglas Broom

title: How dancing can boost mental health
header: What If Dance Could Heal Your Mind? Discover the Therapy Changing Brains and Lives
content:
Dance / Movement Therapy (DMT) — A Simple Guide

  • DMT uses movement to support healing and well-being.
  • It works because body posture and movement affect emotions.
  • DMT helps people with depression, Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s.

Many adults stop dancing and disconnect from their bodies. Yet movement can be a powerful tool for mental health.

What Is DMT?

DMT is more than dancing for fun. It uses movement to:

  • Increase insight and awareness
  • Support emotional balance
  • Improve symptoms in different conditions

DMT often includes:

  • Warm-ups and emotional check-ins
  • Movement themes (like working with emotions)
  • Grounding at the end to reconnect with the present
  • Optional talking, music, drawing or journaling

Why It Works

DMT is based on a simple idea:

Mind and body constantly affect each other.

Changing movement patterns can:

  • Shift emotions
  • Create new ways of thinking
  • Uncover hidden memories or feelings

Benefits Seen in Research

1. Helps with Depression

Studies show DMT reduces depressive symptoms by:

  • Improving mood through movement
  • Helping people see new possibilities

2. Cognitive Improvements in Older Adults

Dance engages the brain deeply. Research found improvements in:

  • Attention and memory
  • Balance and coordination
  • Brain plasticity (ability to grow and change)

3. Parkinson’s Disease Support

Meta-analysis shows dance improves:

  • Executive function (planning and action control)
  • Movement ability

4. Visible Brain Changes

Well-designed studies found dance increased brain volume in areas linked to:

  • Memory
  • Movement control
  • Communication between brain hemispheres

Why DMT Matters

DMT shows that:

  • Movement can change how we think and feel.
  • Posture affects mood and perception.
  • New movement creates new emotional experiences.

Final Thought

DMT reconnects us to our bodies. It offers new ways of feeling, healing and growing — and deserves a bigger place in everyday therapy.
author: Adrianna Mendrek

title: Letting Go Of Things – Life As We Know It Or Do We?
header: When Life Stops Making Sense — That’s When Transformation Begins
content:
Letting Go and Moving Forward

Letting go is hard. We often hold onto things we believe we cannot live without — a job, a relationship, or a picture of the “perfect life.”

But life has a way of revealing the truth. Something that once made you happy may suddenly become the very source of pain. That moment feels like everything is falling apart — but it is also when you begin to wake up.

Waking Up

Many people are realizing life is more than routines. Emotional and spiritual unrest pushes us to look inward.

This inner journey can feel confusing. Awakening sounds beautiful, but it is painful because it involves breaking old beliefs and facing yourself.

The good news is — we are not alone. These experiences happen to many people. We grow faster when we support each other instead of hiding our struggles.

Attachment

We live in a world where attachment feels natural — to habits, people, or identities.

  • We hold on to old thinking
  • We repeat familiar patterns
  • We stay in relationships or roles that keep us stuck

Asking deeper questions shows us uncomfortable truths — but this awareness is necessary for change.

Anger and Fear

Once questioning begins, fear arrives. Life once felt predictable and manageable — now nothing satisfies the soul.

You may feel lost, unsure how to rebuild when you no longer recognize the old picture of your life.

Depression

Sadness can settle in. Things that once excited you — work, social outings, entertainment — no longer feel meaningful.

You may wonder:

“Why can’t I be like everyone else?”

But often, others are simply comfortable living without change — even if they are quietly unhappy.

Letting Go

Letting go means facing the truth that life is temporary — and that is scary.

But letting go also gives you something greater:

A real relationship with yourself.

  • You stop clinging and start accepting
  • You trust life more
  • You discover what you want — not what the world expects from you

Moving Forward

Letting go takes courage. You will fall, feel defeated, and doubt yourself — but what matters is that you rise again.

Letting go is better than living a lie.

Allow truth to break you and rebuild you. Let pain teach compassion. Let fear build bravery.

This message is for anyone searching for their truth:

Don’t give up.

The truth will free you — but first, it frees you from everything holding you back.

Do not fear falling apart. It gives you the chance to rebuild yourself in a way you always wanted.
author: Tamara Khotu

title: Fake Smiles May Be Bad for Your Health
header: What Happens When You Smile… But Don’t Mean It? New Study Reveals.
content:
How Smiling Affects Happiness

We often give a polite smile — at work, in crowds, or when someone tells a joke. But a new study suggests that fake smiling may actually reduce our inner happiness.

Fake vs Real Smiles

Researchers followed bus drivers for two weeks because their work involves constant polite interactions. They observed how their moods changed based on the type of smile they used.

Key findings:

  • On days with forced smiles, moods worsened and drivers became withdrawn.
  • Trying to hide negative feelings made them even stronger.
  • But when drivers created real smiles through positive thoughts or memories, their mood improved.
  • Authentic smiling also increased productivity.

What Does This Mean?

We usually think emotions create facial expressions, but this study shows the reverse is also true — our expressions can influence how we feel.

A genuine smile can lift our happiness. A fake one, without positive feeling behind it, may lower it.

Want to Explore More?

You can test how well you recognize real vs fake smiles by trying emotional intelligence quizzes or observing expressions in daily life.

Lesson: Instead of forcing a smile, try thinking of something pleasant — it may brighten your mood more than the smile itself.

title: How Awe Brings People Together
header: Why Awe Makes You Feel Tiny — and Why That’s Exactly What Your Heart Needs.
content:
Awe Makes Us Feel Smaller — and More Connected

Awe is the feeling we get when we see something amazing — like mountains, art, or a newborn baby. It fills us with wonder and reminds us how big the world is.

Researchers found that awe does more than make us feel good. It actually gives us a “small self” feeling, which makes us less focused on ourselves and more connected to others.

What the Studies Show

  • After people experienced awe, they described themselves as smaller or less important.
  • This happened in different cultures — both in China and the United States.
  • Awe wasn’t tied to sadness or fear — it was unique and uplifting.
  • Chinese participants often felt awe through relationships, while Americans felt awe more through nature.

Awe in Real Life

People visiting a beautiful place like Yosemite drew smaller pictures of themselves compared to people at busy tourist spots. Feeling awe literally changed how they saw themselves.

A lab experiment confirmed the same thing: people who watched an awe-inspiring nature video felt smaller (in a positive way) than people who watched a funny video.

Why the “Small Self” Matters

  • Feeling small through awe doesn’t reduce confidence or social status.
  • It helps us feel closer to others and increases social connection.
  • Different cultures showed this in different ways — Americans added more people to their social circle drawings, while Chinese participants drew closer relationships.

Awe vs Shame

Both awe and shame make us feel small. But there is a difference:

  • Shame lowers self-esteem and makes us withdraw.
  • Awe increases connection and engagement with others.

What This Means for Us

Feeling awe — from nature, music, kindness, or beauty — helps us shift attention away from ourselves. It reminds us we are part of something bigger.

Awe makes us humble, connected, and more open to others.

So seek more awe — watch a sunrise, look at art, spend time in nature, or witness acts of kindness. These moments help us grow and strengthen our relationships.

title: Why being kind makes your child feel good – according to science
header: A Simple Kind Act Can Change Your Mood Instantly — The Science Explains How.
content:
Why Kindness Makes Us Happy

Everyone loves kindness. But people often argue about why we do kind things. Some think kindness is pure and selfless. Others think it is a way to gain favor. Research shows something better — kindness truly makes us happy.

Helping others activates the brain’s reward system. This “warm glow” feeling is similar to the pleasure we get from good food or music. Kindness helps our mood at any age.

Even remembering a past kind act can lift our spirits. Spending money on others also brings more joy than spending it on ourselves.

How Kindness Makes Us Happy

1. Smiles Spread

When we do something kind, others often smile — and their smile affects us, too. Seeing someone happy can make us happy automatically.

2. Fixing Pain Feels Good

We feel connected to others, especially close friends and family. Helping them when they are sad can make us feel relief and a sense of doing something right. Even supporting big causes like poverty or climate action can improve our mood.

3. Kindness Builds Connection

Kind acts help us make and grow relationships — buying a small gift, offering help, or volunteering. Stronger friendships and meaningful connections naturally improve happiness.

4. Kindness Strengthens Identity

Most of us want to see ourselves as kind people. Helping others makes us feel proud and complete. Kindness also feels stronger when it matches our personality — like animal lovers rescuing pets or artists supporting galleries.

5. Kindness Comes Back

Kindness often leads to more kindness. People remember good deeds and may help you later. Kindness can spread through groups — one act can inspire many.

Finally, kindness and happiness feed each other. Being kind makes you happy — and being happy makes you kinder.
author: Jo Cutler

title: Tips On How To Maintain A Healthy Relationship While Traveling
header: Save Your Trip and Your Relationship: Simple Rules Happy Couples Follow.
content:
Traveling Together Without Relationship Stress

Traveling with your soulmate is fun — but spending all day together can sometimes create tension. Here are simple tips to keep the relationship happy and strong during travel.

1. Don’t Expect Perfection

Everyone has flaws. Instead of focusing on your partner’s weaknesses, remember you also have your own. Appreciate the good qualities that made you fall in love in the first place.

2. Plan Together

Ask what each person wants from the trip. Share goals and expectations. Look for compromise or choose options that work for both of you.

3. Use Your Strengths

Each person is good at different things. One may navigate well, the other may talk easily with locals. Support each other and accept help when needed.

4. Share Duties Fairly

Some tasks are boring but necessary. Take turns — for example, “Today I do it, tomorrow you do.” Fairness prevents frustration.

5. Support Each Other

Bad moods happen. Cheer your partner up or take over tasks when they need it. They will do the same for you later.

6. Rest When Tired

Lack of sleep makes people irritable. If either of you is exhausted, stop and rest. A few hours of sleep can fix many problems.

7. Diffuse Tension Playfully

When things feel tense, do something light — dance in the street, hug, or smile. Small moments of fun can dissolve conflict.

8. Keep Showing Love

Don’t take each other for granted. Say “I love you,” give small gifts, listen, and show appreciation. Love grows when we actively care.

With patience, teamwork, and affection, traveling together can build — not break — your relationship.
author: Aleksander

title: Things You Shouldn’t Ignore To Be Really Happy In Life
header: Why Your Happiness Keeps Fading — and the Practices That Bring It Back.
content:
Simple Ways To Stay Happy

Happiness is a state of mind. But daily stress, comparison, and busy living often push us away from it. To stay happy, we have to work at it — one small habit at a time.

1. Accept That You Want To Grow

Ask yourself what you want to improve — laziness, fear, envy, or procrastination. Most people know their flaws but avoid accepting them. Once you accept what needs to change, life already becomes lighter.

2. Try Vipassana – Calm Your Mind

Vipassana is a 10-day silent meditation practice that helps clear deep emotional patterns. The silence isn’t the hardest part — facing yourself is. You only need three things to attend: time, effort, and willpower.

3. Be Here Now

Live in the present moment. Eat while eating, walk while walking, breathe while breathing. When mind and body move together, peace comes naturally.

4. Karma Always Works

Give good, get good. Do kind actions with a pure heart — not only to receive the benefit back, but to make someone’s life easier.

5. Move Your Body

You don’t need to become a bodybuilder — just stay active. Walk, dance, stretch, do yoga, or join a class. One hour of movement a day helps release stress and clear your mind.

6. Remember Nothing Is Permanent

Just like seasons change, emotions and situations change too. Sadness doesn’t last forever — and neither does joy. Find balance and flow with life.

7. Have a Healthy Outlet

Find activities that reduce stress. Avoid alcohol or shopping as escape — they push feelings deeper. Try volunteering, learning something new, creating, or helping others.

8. Practice Love and Kindness

Love deeply. Be kind to people who can’t give you anything back. Kindness purifies the heart and fills life with meaning.

The best way to live life is in happiness — and happiness grows when you work on it daily.
author: Ayesha Majid

title: Leisurely Walk In Your Daily Life Is So Important To Make You More Productive And Happy
header: The Walk That Quieted My Mind—and Reminded Me What Really Matters.
content:
Don’t Miss The Little Things

In a fast world full of distractions, small details often disappear. We stop noticing them, even though they matter.

I often walk to a nearby sports complex. Even when I had a job, I still went. Sometimes I leave home filled with doubt, but I usually return lighter and happier. Does the walk give me answers? Not always — but it helps me forget the questions for a while.

The footpath is quiet while the road is crowded with traffic. I appreciate that where I live, sidewalks are actually used for walking. No bikes or cars rushing behind you.

On the road, I see many people driving with one hand and checking their phones with the other. What could be so urgent? A text? A call? Honestly, everything can wait when you are driving.

At the sports complex, I walk or run. I notice an elderly couple sitting in the park, simply enjoying the sunlight. They don’t speak — just smile quietly. Some couples are truly beautiful to watch.

Today, I didn’t carry many worries. I did, however, feel stuck — a writer’s block. But look at the magic: without forcing it, the words came. My mind relaxed, and my fingers kept typing.

Don’t miss the small moments life offers because you’re glued to a screen. A lot can wait.

When you take a walk, you may leave home with worries — but try to return without them.

Unwind your mind. Be more productive. Be happy.
author: Bhavna Sultana

title: Self-Esteem Tips And Tricks To Keep Yourself Positive
header: Old habits are draining your confidence—here’s how to break free.
content:
Boosting Self-Esteem

Self-esteem is feeling good about who you are and what you do. It helps you live without constant self-criticism or negative thinking. When you value yourself, you stop over-checking every action and use your energy to grow, connect, and achieve.

If you want to improve your self-esteem, here are simple steps.

1. Assess Yourself Fairly

Pause and take an honest look at your life — your personality, habits, work, and relationships.

  • Write down your strengths and weaknesses.
  • Notice what you like about yourself.
  • See areas you want to improve.

No one is all good or all bad — knowing both sides helps you grow.

2. Refresh Your Appearance

Sometimes a small change boosts confidence.

  • Try a new hairstyle.
  • Update your clothes or accessories.
  • Take care of your smile — even simple dental care helps.

Looking after yourself often improves how you feel inside.

3. Write Down Your Experiences

We all carry good and bad memories. Writing about them helps you understand how past events shape your feelings. This awareness supports healing and growth.

4. Work on Bad Habits

Sometimes low self-esteem comes from habits we know are holding us back.

  • Seek help if you struggle with addiction.
  • Join support groups or talk to a therapist.
  • Take action to replace harmful habits with healthier ones.

5. Use Real Affirmations

Positive self-talk works best when it is specific and true to your life.

  • Use affirmations based on your strengths.
  • Skip vague statements — make them real and personal.
  • Repeat them to guide your mindset toward growth.

Building self-esteem is a process — small steps over time make a big difference.
author: Dixie Somers

title: Ways Happiness Can Hurt You
header: Can happiness backfire? New science reveals the surprising dark side.
content:
Can Feeling Good Ever Be Bad?

Happiness is often praised for boosting health, motivation, connection, and well-being. But new research shows that too much happiness, or happiness at the wrong time, can actually harm us.

Here are four ways happiness can backfire — and how to build healthier balance.

1. Too Much Happiness Can Reduce Creativity and Safety

Happiness in moderation helps thinking and problem-solving. But research finds:

  • Very intense happiness may reduce creativity.
  • Too much positivity can make us ignore risks.
  • People in “happiness overdrive” may drink too much, eat excessively, or make unsafe choices.

Balance matters — not too little, not too much.

2. Happiness Doesn’t Fit Every Situation

Each emotion has a purpose. For example:

  • Anger helps us push through obstacles.
  • Fear protects us from danger.
  • Sadness signals loss and invites support.

Happiness signals success and tells us to slow down. But in competition or serious moments, happiness can hurt performance or feel inappropriate.

3. Not All Happiness Is Healthy

Happiness has different forms. Some connect us to others — some make us self-focused.

Example: Pride.

  • Healthy pride from effort or achievement is good.
  • Excess pride can harm relationships, increase aggression, and weaken empathy.

Some positive emotions may actually disconnect us from others when taken too far.

4. Chasing Happiness Can Make You Unhappy

Research shows that the harder we try to “be happy,” the easier it is to feel disappointed.

When happiness becomes a goal or competition, people often:

  • Set unrealistic expectations.
  • Feel worse when they fall short.
  • Experience more stress or sadness.

So How Do We Find Healthy Happiness?

  • Allow happiness in the right amount.
  • Notice which situations call for which emotions.
  • Let yourself feel discomfort — sadness, anger, and fear also have value.
  • Stop trying to force happiness.
  • Practice acceptance and kindness toward yourself and others.

Real happiness grows from emotional balance — not from chasing constant positivity.
